weeks.title: We Love Because He First Loved Us
weeks.theme: Love is not something squeezed out of me; it flows in from God and then flows out again.
group: Read 1 John 4:16-21. How does John link “God loves us” with “we love our brothers and sisters”?
Have you ever tried so hard to love someone that you ran completely dry? What was missing at the time?
This week, which hard-to-love person do you want to love the way Jesus loves you?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, write a handwritten card to someone who loved you during a season of weakness. Name one specific thing they did and the difference it made in your life. Before you write, thank God for the love he brought you through them; after you send it, pray for them. If you can, write a second card to someone who needs to be loved right now.

lessons.title: Love Doesn’t Start with Me
lessons.hear:
Starting this week, we enter the “life” stage. Over the past few weeks we have exposed the root of self-centered socializing. Now we ask: where does selfless love come from? The apostle John gives an answer that is both very simple and very deep: “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

Notice the order in that sentence. It is not “we love first, so God loves us.” God goes first. Love does not begin in our hearts; it begins in God’s heart. The moon gives off no light of its own—every bit of its glow comes from the sun. In the same way, we are not power plants that generate love; we are mirrors that reflect it. If the moon tried to shine on its own, it would stay dark. All it has to do is turn toward the sun.

The Old Testament prophet said it long ago: “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness” (Jeremiah 31:3). God’s love is not a reward for our performance; it is the foundation of our existence. John writes, “We know and have believed the love which God has for us” (1 John 4:16). To know is for the mind to understand; to believe is to lean your whole weight on it. Many people know that God loves the world, but don’t believe that God loves them right now. So they go begging for love from people, and their relationships become tense and hungry.

But John doesn’t stop there. He goes on to say that if someone says “I love God” but hates his brother, “he is a liar” (1 John 4:20). Love received from God turns sour if it stays inside us and never flows out. People who are truly loved will inevitably love others. Love is like a river: its source is God, the riverbed is me, and it flows toward everyone around me.
lessons.light: The order of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others. Only when we are loved by God can we accept ourselves; only when we accept ourselves are we free to love others. This is where “life” begins in the five-fold change: not by improving our skills first, but by letting God’s love move in. Selflessness is not emptiness; it is being filled with Christ’s love.
think: In 1 John 4:16-21, how are “love” and “fear” related?
Do I merely “know” that God loves me, or do I truly “believe” he loves me right now?
Today, toward which person near me can I let God’s love flow?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me first—loving me before I knew you, when I was not lovable at all. I keep begging people for love because I forget that your love is enough. Today let me not only know but truly believe that you love me, and let this love flow out from me to the people around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This morning, take three minutes to slowly read 1 John 4:19 three times. Then think of one person you will see today and say to the Lord in your heart, “You love me, and I will love them.”
lessons.quick: We are not power plants of love but the moon, reflecting God’s love.
text: We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.
In this, love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so we are in this world.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.
We love him, because he first loved us.
If a man says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?
This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother.

lessons.title: Love Isn’t Squeezed Out
lessons.hear:
A sister who led a small group had one member who was especially hard to be around: he was often late, quick to criticize, and liked to vent in the group chat. She kept reminding herself to “be loving.” Before every meeting she gritted her teeth and endured; afterward she was too drained to talk. Six months later she told her pastor, “I have no love left to give.”

This is the old mindset of many Christians: love is an effort, like squeezing a nearly empty tube of toothpaste—the harder you squeeze, the flatter it gets. We think loving people means using willpower to suppress irritation and forcing ourselves to be nice. That kind of love can hold out for a while, but not for a lifetime. In the end it either explodes or goes numb.

God’s view is completely different. Paul says that “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5). “Poured” is a word of abundance, like a downpour on dry ground. Love is not something I squeeze out; it is something God pours in. And God gave his love at the most unlovable moment: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Eventually that sister changed the order. Instead of gritting her teeth before meetings, she first quietly received: “Lord, you loved me while I was still a sinner.” She found that when she remembered she had once been the “hard-to-love person,” her heart softened. She began praying specifically for that group member, and later learned he was under enormous pressure at home. Love didn’t make the problem disappear, but she was no longer fighting alone. And of course, if you feel worn out in body and soul for a long time, stopping to rest, asking co-workers to share the load, or even seeking counseling are also gifts of God’s grace.
lessons.light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Loving in your own strength is self-centered effort, and it eventually runs dry; letting the Holy Spirit pour love in is selfless receiving, and it never runs out. Selflessness is not having nothing—it is entering the limitless. My love is limited; God’s love is limitless. Receive first, then give: that is the order of the life of love.
think: In Romans 5:5-8, in what condition were we when God’s love was shown to us?
In which relationship am I trying to love by “squeezing the toothpaste tube”?
Before I face that person today, how will I first receive God’s love?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, pour God’s love into my heart once again today. I confess that I often try to love others in my own strength, until I am exhausted and bitter. Remind me that the Lord died for me while I was still a sinner. Fill me with yourself first, and then let me love the person I find hard to love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone you’ve been “exhausted loving” lately. Today, don’t rush to do anything; first pray specifically for them for five minutes. Then consider what unseen burden they might be carrying.
lessons.quick: Love isn’t something I squeeze out; it’s something the Holy Spirit pours in.
text: and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

lessons.title: Love as He Loved Me
lessons.hear:
Jesus called this a “new” commandment. But wasn’t “love your neighbor” already in the Law of Moses? So what is new? The newness is in the second half: “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” (John 13:34). The old standard was “as yourself”; the new standard is “as the Lord.” The measuring stick for love has changed from me to Jesus.

So how did Jesus love us? On the very night he said this, he had just knelt and washed his disciples’ feet—including Judas, who was about to betray him, and Peter, who was about to deny him three times. His love had three marks: he took the initiative, not waiting for people to deserve it; he was concrete, not just talk; and he paid a price, loving all the way to the cross.

Today, let’s love one person by these three marks:

1. Take the initiative: don’t wait for the other person to say hello first, apologize first, or show concern first.
2. Be concrete: a meal, a phone call, a ride, a sentence like “I remember what you told me last time.”
3. Pay a small price: spend your time, set aside your pride, or give up your convenience.

Jesus went on to say, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). The world may not read the Bible, but it reads us. A neighbor may never set foot in a church, but he will remember the person who showed up to help when he moved. Love is a Christian’s clearest business card. Today, let someone recognize Jesus in you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example. What makes the new commandment “new” is that it raises the standard of love from “I think that’s enough” to “the way the Lord loves me.” That standard seems too high—but precisely because the Lord has already loved me this way, I have the strength to love like this. The “2” in 920 is the person you will take the initiative to love today.
think: In John 13:34-35, what is “new” about the new commandment? What is the purpose of this love?
Do I usually wait for others to be kind to me before I respond with love?
Whom will I love today with initiative, in concrete ways, and at some cost?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you loved me first when I did not deserve it, loved me concretely, and even gave your life for me. Today I want to love someone the way you love me. Give me the courage to take the first step and a heart willing to pay the price, so that they will recognize you in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Choose one person today and take the initiative to do something concrete for them that costs you some time—buy them a coffee, run an errand for them—and say in your heart, “As the Lord loves me, so I will love them.”
lessons.quick: The measuring stick changes from “as yourself” to “as the Lord”: take the initiative, be concrete, pay the price.
text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

lessons.title: Forgiven Little, Loving Little
lessons.hear:
Simon the Pharisee invited Jesus to his home for dinner. On the surface the meal was respectable, yet it lacked the most basic courtesies for a guest in that culture: no water to wash his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head. Just then a woman known throughout the town as a “sinner” came in, wet Jesus’ feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment. Simon coldly passed judgment in his heart.

So Jesus told a parable. Two people owed a lender money—one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty—and the lender forgave them both. Which one would love him more? Simon answered correctly: “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” Then Jesus said, “her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little” (Luke 7:47).

The problem here is not that Simon had fewer sins. It is that he felt he had fewer sins. He had put himself in the judge’s seat, so he could not feel grace; and without feeling grace, no love could flow from him. Today, take an honest look: when I am cold, critical, or unwilling to get close to someone, is it because deep down I am saying, “I’m not like him”? When I see someone make a mistake in the group chat, is my first reaction compassion—or a secret sigh of relief that I’m better?

The way to adjust is not to force myself to love a little more, but to come back before grace and see again how much I have been forgiven. No one taught that woman how to love. She simply knew she had been forgiven, and love came pouring out. When we see again how great the cross is, the love in our hearts grows great again.
lessons.light: Simon’s self-centeredness was taking the judge’s seat—leaving his proper place and grasping God’s power. Humility is returning to our proper place: admitting that I, like that woman, am a sinner who has received grace. Pride dries up love; humility lets grace flow back. When I love little, the answer is not to try harder but to become humbler.
think: In Luke 7:44-46, which actions of Simon and of the woman does Jesus contrast?
Before whom have I recently acted like Simon, secretly thinking, “I’m not like him”?
Today, how will I count again the Lord’s forgiveness of me, so that love can flow again?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I am often like Simon, judging others in my heart while forgetting how much I owed. Thank you for forgiving my many sins. Let me see the grace of the cross again, step down from the judge’s seat, and with a grateful heart love those I once looked down on. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, write down three ways the Lord has forgiven you and borne with you. Then think of someone you secretly look down on, and tomorrow take the initiative to say something sincerely kind to them.
lessons.quick: When we love little, it’s often because we’ve forgotten how much we’ve been forgiven.
text: Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He said, “Teacher, say on.”
“A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?”
Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” He said to him, “You have judged correctly.”

Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head.
You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.
You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”

lessons.title: Love Rooted and Grounded
lessons.hear:
How much fruit a tree bears depends on how deep its roots go. When a typhoon hits, the tree with the fullest branches doesn’t necessarily stay standing; the tree with deep roots does. Paul prayed for the believers in Ephesus that Christ would dwell in their hearts, so that they would be “rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17). The life of love is not a single emotional moment but a process of putting down roots.

This week we have seen that the source of love is God: God loved us first, the Holy Spirit pours love into our hearts, Jesus becomes our measure of love, and the forgiveness of the cross makes love flow again. These truths need to be repeated again and again, because we so easily slip back into the old road of “squeezing out love by ourselves.” Roots grow where no one can see: in quiet moments before God each day, letting his love soak in.

Paul asked for one more thing: that we “may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth” (Ephesians 3:18). Notice “with all the saints.” God’s love is not something one person can fully grasp behind closed doors. It is in our relationships with brothers and sisters that we see the width and length and height and depth of this love. Your experience shows me one side of his love; my experience shows you another.

So today, pass this love on. Not by preaching a sermon, but by doing what Paul did: praying for someone. You can use this passage to pray for a friend, a small group member, or a family member, and then tell them, “Today I prayed this for you.” Many people have never in their lives heard of anyone praying for them like this. When they learn that they are loved by God and remembered by you, the roots of love begin to grow down into another life.
lessons.light: The “2” in 235 is becoming spiritual companions with selfless people. The roots of love only grow deep in fellowship, because we comprehend Christ’s love “with all the saints.” Repetition lets the truth take root in me; multiplication lets the same roots grow in someone else. Intercession is the quietest yet most powerful form of multiplication.
think: In Ephesians 3:16-19, what does Paul ask for on behalf of the believers?
This week, at what moment did I most genuinely experience being “loved first by God”?
For whom will I pray this prayer, and how will I let them know?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, strengthen me in my inner being through your Spirit, and let Christ dwell in my heart so that my love is rooted and grounded. Let me comprehend, together with my brothers and sisters, how wide and long and high and deep the love of Christ is. I also bring a friend before you—please let them know that you love them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, use Ephesians 3:16-19 to pray for a friend or small group member. Then send them a message saying, “Today I prayed this passage for you,” and include the verses.
lessons.quick: The life of love is not a single moment of feeling but a lifetime of putting down roots—roots in God’s love.
text: that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,
may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth,
and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

weeks.keyText: We love him, because he first loved us.

weeks.title: Love Is Patient and Kind
weeks.theme: Patience and kindness are love’s two hands: one bears with others, the other reaches out to give.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 13:1-4. According to Paul, what becomes of gifts and sacrifice without love?
In your relationships, which hand is more likely to pull back—patience or kindness?
This week, toward which person who exhausts your patience are you willing to reach out once with a hand of kindness?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, prepare a small kindness for someone who often makes you lose your patience: a box of fruit, a card, or taking the initiative to help them with something. Before you go, read “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11), and ask the Lord for a gentle heart. Afterward, thank God: his patience with you is longer than yours with anyone.

lessons.title: Without Love, Everything Is Zero
lessons.hear:
First Corinthians 13 is often read at weddings, but Paul originally wrote it to a church full of quarrels. The Corinthian believers had plenty of gifts—tongues, preaching, knowledge—yet they split into factions, compared themselves with one another, and looked down on each other. So Paul wrote: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1).

Picture a concert. Gongs and cymbals have an important place in an orchestra, but if all you hear all night is their crashing, it becomes noise. A person can be eloquent, highly capable, great at running events, even extremely generous—but without love, in relationships they are just noise. Paul uses three “if … but don’t have love” statements in a row, and his conclusion is: “I am nothing” and “it profits me nothing.” Add up gifts, knowledge, and sacrifice, multiply by zero, and you still get zero.

So what does love look like? Paul’s very first phrase is “Love is patient and is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4). Interestingly, he doesn’t begin by saying love is passion or deep feeling; he begins by saying love can bear. Patience means not giving up on people despite their weakness, slowness, and offenses. Kindness means still actively doing good in front of such people.

It is as if love has two hands. One is the hand that receives, catching the difficulties others throw at us. The other is the hand that gives, passing good things along. Patience without kindness turns love into teeth-gritting endurance; kindness without patience makes love withdraw the first time it is let down. Only when both hands reach out together is it the love of Christ.
lessons.light: The Bible is my standard. First Corinthians 13 is not a romantic poem; it is a mirror that exposes the self-centered life. Self-centered people prove themselves through gifts and abilities; selfless people let love be the motive for everything. The “9” in 920—the fruit of the Spirit—must finally be seen in how we bear and how we give.
think: In 1 Corinthians 13:1-3, what things does Paul list as worthless without love?
In what area am I very capable, yet may have become a “clanging cymbal” in my relationships?
To whom can I extend both the hand of patience and the hand of kindness today?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often try to prove myself through ability, eloquence, and effort, forgetting that without love everything comes to zero. Put your patient and kind love in my heart, so that in my relationships today I don’t make noise but sound the harmony of love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in one conversation or one group chat, deliberately say one less thing that shows yourself off and one more thing that shows care for the other person.
lessons.quick: Gifts plus abilities, multiplied by “no love,” still equal zero.
text: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.
Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,

lessons.title: Kind to the Unthankful
lessons.hear:
A sister working at a tech company was always putting out fires for the coworker next to her: teaching him software, finishing his reports, putting in a good word for him with the manager. Yet he never said thank you, and in one meeting he even took all the credit for himself. Furious, she wrote in her journal, “I’m never being nice to him again.”

This is our old mindset: kindness is a transaction. You’re good to me, I’ll be good to you; if you’re not grateful, I pull back. It sounds fair, but Jesus said, “If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same” (Luke 6:33). If our kindness only goes to people who pay us back, it is no different from the world’s give-and-take.

God’s view is higher: “he is kind toward the unthankful and evil” (Luke 6:35). Every day God makes the sun shine on people who never thank him, gives them breath, and gives them the opportunity to repent. We ourselves are among those “unthankful” people, yet we live in his kindness every day. That is why Jesus said, “Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful” (Luke 6:36).

But kindness doesn’t mean letting people use you. After praying, that sister did two things. She privately and gently explained to her coworker that she had done that report, and she hoped next time they could put both their names on it. At the same time, she still lent a hand when he was truly stuck. She discovered that kindness and boundaries can exist together. Boundaries kept her from being used; kindness kept her from becoming bitter. She no longer did it for his payback, but for her heavenly Father.
lessons.light: Self-centered kindness is an investment that expects a return; selfless kindness is sowing seed and leaving the harvest to God. To let Jesus reign is to refuse to let other people’s ingratitude define who I am, and to let the Father’s mercy define me instead. Love is not without boundaries, but the purpose of boundaries is to protect the relationship, not to retaliate.
think: In Luke 6:32-36, what marks the “children of the Most High”?
Do I keep a “ledger” in my heart, tracking who owes me thanks?
Toward someone who is never grateful, how can I be both kind and appropriately bounded?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you are kind to the unthankful and the evil, and you are kind to me every day. Forgive me for so often being good only to people who pay me back. Make me merciful as you are merciful, so that others’ ingratitude cannot steal my kindness; and give me wisdom to know when to reach out and when to gently state a boundary. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do a small kindness for someone who never says thank you, without expecting any response. If needed, also prepare a gentle but clear sentence stating a boundary.
lessons.quick: Being good only to those who repay you is just social custom; being kind to the unthankful is being like the Father.
text: “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.
If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same.
If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive back as much.
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.
“Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.

lessons.title: Patient Toward All
lessons.hear:
Paul gave the church in Thessalonica a very practical “relational prescription”: “Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Notice that he doesn’t give everyone the same medicine. The disorderly need a gentle reminder, the faint-hearted need encouragement, the weak need support—and everyone needs patience.

Patience is like a gardener tending a fruit tree. He doesn’t chop it down because it bore no fruit this year; he loosens the soil, adds fertilizer, and waits for the season. The people around us are the same: the new coworker who is always a step behind, the elderly relative who tells the same stories, the cousin who keeps forwarding rumors in the family chat, the friend who is always late. They are all still growing in God’s garden, and God has sent us to be their gardeners for a season.

Today’s practice is concrete: choose one person who often makes you lose your patience, and treat them with both hands.

1. The hand of patience: when they make the same mistake again, take a deep breath first and say in your heart, “The Lord waits for me like this too.” Don’t roll your eyes, don’t sigh, don’t correct them right away.
2. The hand of kindness: then do something good for them—make the font bigger on an older relative’s phone, or when someone forwards a rumor in the group, send them the correct information privately instead of calling them out in public.

Paul continues, “See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone” (1 Thessalonians 5:15). A caution: patience is not tolerating harm. If someone’s behavior involves violence, harassment, fraud, or extortion, safety comes first—seek help from someone you trust or from professionals. The patience the Bible speaks of gives people time to grow, within God’s protection and wisdom.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks. Impatience often means valuing “getting things done” over “people growing up.” The root of patience is remembering how patiently God has waited for me; the hand of kindness turns that patience into concrete good. Change begins with me: when I slow down first, others have room to grow.
think: What kinds of people does 1 Thessalonians 5:14 list, and what different kind of love does each need?
Who most easily makes me lose my patience, and how do I usually show it when I do?
Today, what will my “hand of patience” and my “hand of kindness” look like toward that person?
lessons.speak: Lord, how patient you are with me, waiting again and again for me to turn back. Give me a gentle heart today, so that when I face the person who makes me impatient, I can first pause and remember how you wait for me, and then reach out in kindness. Also give me wisdom to discern when I need to protect myself and others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, with the person who most easily makes you lose your patience, at least once hold back from sighing or interrupting—and also do one small good thing for them.
lessons.quick: Support for the weak, encouragement for the faint-hearted, patience toward all.
text: We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.
See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.

lessons.title: Jonah’s Booth
lessons.hear:
Jonah is the most “honest” prophet in the Bible, because he told God straight out why he hadn’t wanted to go to Nineveh: “I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness” (Jonah 4:2). It wasn’t that he didn’t understand God’s patience and kindness. He just didn’t want God to give them to people he hated.

We are a lot like him. We want God to be endlessly patient with us and especially kind about our failures. But when God is equally kind to the person who hurt us or the person we look down on, we feel uneasy. Jonah went outside the city, made himself a booth, and sat in its shade “until he might see what would become of the city” (Jonah 4:5). He was waiting for someone else to fail.

Take an honest look: is there a “Jonah’s booth” somewhere in my social circle? Maybe it’s watching coldly from the sidelines when someone messes up in a group chat. Maybe it’s a flicker of satisfaction when I hear that an old classmate is struggling. Maybe it’s sulking when someone at church I don’t like gets praised. We gladly receive patience and kindness, but we are stingy about giving them away.

Yet the most beautiful thing about this book is that God was patient with Jonah too. He didn’t give up on the angry prophet. He arranged a vine, a worm, and an east wind, and twice gently asked, “Is it right for you to be angry?” In the end he said, “Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city” (Jonah 4:11)? God treated Jonah with kindness so that Jonah could learn kindness. The road to adjustment is to step out of the booth, accept God’s patience toward me, and let that patience flow to the people I don’t like.
lessons.light: Jonah’s booth is the grandstand of the self-centered life: sitting up high, deciding who deserves grace. That is leaving our proper place and trying to take God’s. Humility is returning to our proper place—admitting that grace was never something anyone deserved, not even me. God opposes the proud, yet he keeps patiently waiting for the proud to turn back.
think: In Jonah 4:1-11, in what ways does God deal gently with Jonah?
Is there someone I secretly hope will “get what’s coming to them”?
Today, how can I step out of the booth and pray a blessing over that person?
lessons.speak: God, you are gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness. I love it when you treat me this way, yet I often don’t want you to treat others the same. Forgive me for sitting in my booth waiting for others to fail. Thank you for still speaking patiently to me. Today I choose to step out and bless that person. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray specifically for three blessings for someone you secretly don’t want to see do well. If appropriate, also give them a sincere greeting.
lessons.quick: We gladly receive God’s patience but are stingy in passing it on—step out of Jonah’s booth.
text: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

He prayed to the LORD, and said, “Please, LORD, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and you relent of doing harm.
Therefore now, LORD, take, I beg you, my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
The LORD said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
Then Jonah went out of the city and sat on the east side of the city, and there made himself a booth and sat under it in the shade, until he might see what would become of the city.
The LORD God prepared a vine and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
But God prepared a worm at dawn the next day, and it chewed on the vine so that it withered.

When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he was faint and requested for himself that he might die. He said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”
The LORD said, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night and perished in a night.

Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”

lessons.title: A Showcase of the Lord’s Patience
lessons.hear:
Late in life, looking back, Paul said something astonishing: “However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). He wasn’t claiming to be the most patient person; he was saying he was the person who had received the most patience. He had been a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent, yet Christ did not give up on him. His whole life became a showcase of the Lord’s patience.

This week we have learned love’s two hands: patience and kindness. We have seen that without love everything comes to zero; we have learned to be kind to the unthankful, to be patient toward all, and to step out of Jonah’s booth. These lessons need repeating, because impatience and score-keeping always creep back. Every time we lose our patience, the best adjustment is to remember: how patient has the Lord been with me?

In fact, your own story is a testimony too. Maybe your parents prayed for you for years, waiting for you to come back. Maybe a small group leader accepted you when you were at your least lovable. Maybe God has lifted you up again after you fell time after time. That patience was not wasted—it is why you are here today.

So today, pass this testimony on. Find someone and tell them, “Someone was very patient with me once, and it changed me.” You could also go and thank the person who was patient with you. When we tell the story of how we were borne with, others glimpse God’s patience in it—and someone who is bearing with a difficult person and about to give up may find fresh strength.
lessons.light: Multiplication begins with testimony. “For an example of those who were going to believe”—the story of how I have been borne with is a gift to the next generation. The “3” in 235 is spiritual parents and children: what matters most for spiritual parents is often not how much they teach, but how long they are patient. Change begins with me, and it is passed on through me.
think: In 1 Timothy 1:12-16, how does Paul describe who he used to be and who he became?
Who in my life has been especially patient with me, and what did that patience change in me?
Today, whom will I tell this story of being borne with—or whom will I go and thank?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for displaying your patience in me; I too am a showcase of your grace. Thank you for bringing me to this day through the people who were patient with me. Make me a vessel of patience in other people’s lives, passing on the kindness I have received to the next person. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to or call someone who was once patient with you, and thank them specifically. Or share in your small group a story of “someone who was patient with me.”
lessons.quick: I am a showcase of the Lord’s patience; my story of being borne with is hope for someone else.
text: I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service,
although I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.

weeks.title: Love Doesn’t Seek Its Own Way
weeks.theme: Love looks like a string of “nots”—it doesn’t envy, doesn’t brag, isn’t proud, keeps no account of wrongs—because self is no longer at the center.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4-6. Which of these “nots” is most often tested in your relationships?
Do you keep a “ledger of favors” in your heart? How does it affect your relationship with a particular person?
This week, in what small matter are you willing to put the other person’s good ahead of your own?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, when you share a meal with family or friends, practice “not seeking your own way”: let others choose the restaurant and order first, give the best seats to the elders, and offer to pay or to clean up. Before you head out, pray, “Lord, let me see their needs today.” When you get home, take stock: at what moment, when you let someone else benefit, did your own heart feel free? Give thanks for it.

lessons.title: A String of “Nots”
lessons.hear:
Someone once described a sculptor’s craft like this: the statue is already inside the stone; he simply chips away everything that isn’t the statue. When Paul describes love, he uses a similar method. With a long string of “nots,” he chips away the stone of the self-centered life so that the likeness of Christ can emerge: “Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil” (1 Corinthians 13:4-5).

Notice that all these “nots” share a common core: “me.” Envy happens because someone else got what I wanted. Bragging is wanting others to notice me. Pride is feeling that I’m above you. The opposite of not seeking its own way is calculating my own advantage in everything. Being easily provoked happens because I was offended. Keeping an account of evil means writing down, entry by entry, everything others owe me. Every “not” chips away one stone of self-centeredness.

The heart of the list is this week’s memory verse: love “doesn’t seek its own way.” This doesn’t mean we have no needs or feelings. It means my own advantage is no longer the starting point of my relationships. Think of a good basketball player. Of course he wants to score, but he cares more about the team winning, so he is willing to pass the ball to a teammate who has a better shot.

The last line is positive: love “doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). Selfless love is not being a pushover or blurring right and wrong. Love doesn’t secretly gloat when others fall, and it won’t lie just to keep the peace. It rejoices in the truth, because the truth sets people free.
lessons.light: Self-centeredness is the root of humanity’s fall, and every “not” in 1 Corinthians 13 strikes at that root. Selflessness is not erasing the self; it is inviting the self down from the throne and letting Jesus reign. When “I” am no longer the center, envy, bragging, and score-keeping run out of fuel.
think: In 1 Corinthians 13:4-6, which “nots” concern our words, and which concern our thoughts?
Of these “nots,” which “stone” is biggest in me?
Where today can I deliberately chip away one of them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your love does not seek its own way—you even gave yourself up for me. Chip away the self-centered stones in my heart: envy, bragging, pride, keeping score. Let your likeness come out in me, so that people can see you in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: In one conversation today, deliberately don’t mention your own achievements or experiences. Focus on listening to the other person, and before you finish, ask a question that shows you care about them.
lessons.quick: Every “not” of love chips away a stone centered on “me.”
text: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;

lessons.title: Bearing the Weaknesses of the Weak
lessons.hear:
A sister doing graduate studies in Australia shared an apartment with a younger student who had just left home for the first time. The younger girl was homesick and not very good at looking after herself; she often forgot to take out the trash and would call her family crying in the middle of the night. At first the older sister was patient, but she grew more and more irritated: “I can barely finish my own thesis—why should I have to take care of her?” She started wearing headphones, shutting her door, and treating her roommate as if she were invisible.

This is our natural old mindset: looking after yourself first is the smart thing to do; other people’s weaknesses are their own business. The world often says, “You have to love yourself first before you have the energy to care about others.” There is some truth in that, but if it becomes the governing principle of life, eventually everyone shuts their door and no one carries anyone.

Paul says, “Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Romans 15:1). Notice the word “ought”—in God’s kingdom, strength exists to support the weak. Think of a hiking team: the fastest climber doesn’t race to the summit alone; he stays with the group and helps carry packs. Paul gives the reason: “For even Christ didn’t please himself” (Romans 15:3). If he had only pleased himself, he would never have gone to the cross.

After praying, that sister decided to cook dinner with her roommate once a week and, at the same time, agree on how to split the chores. She was also honest: “I’m racing to finish my thesis and need quiet at night—can we agree to keep it down after eleven?” Bearing others’ weaknesses doesn’t mean carrying an unlimited load; it means walking alongside them with love and with boundaries. A few months later, the younger girl started going to church with her. That small apartment became her first home in a foreign land.
lessons.light: The “strength” God gives me is not for proving myself but for supporting others. This is the selfless way of seeing: my time, abilities, and experience are all entrusted to me by God and prepared for others. People matter more than tasks—the thesis must be written, but the homesick person beside me is also the “2” God has placed in my life.
think: In Romans 15:1-3, whose example does Paul use to illustrate “not pleasing ourselves”?
In what area am I “strong,” yet using that strength only to look after myself?
Who around me is weak right now, and how can I bear with them with both love and boundaries?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you did not please yourself; you bore my weakness and my shame. Forgive me for so often putting my own convenience first and shutting the door on others’ weaknesses. Help me use the strength you have given me to support others, and give me wisdom to walk alongside them with both love and boundaries. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find someone who is weaker than you in some area—a new coworker, an elderly person, a new roommate or church member—and take the initiative to offer one concrete form of help, such as teaching them something or going with them to take care of an errand.
lessons.quick: In God’s kingdom, the strong exist to support the weak; even Christ didn’t please himself.
text: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.
For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”

lessons.title: Seeking the Other Person’s Good
lessons.hear:
Paul says, “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good” (1 Corinthians 10:24). He was originally addressing a very everyday issue: eating meat that had been offered to idols. Paul knew that eating or not eating made no difference to his relationship with God; he had that freedom. But he would rather give up his freedom than cause someone with weak faith to stumble. Love that doesn’t seek its own way is usually trained in choices that look small like this.

Abraham in the Old Testament gives us a beautiful example too. When his herdsmen quarreled with those of his nephew Lot, Abraham, as the elder, had every right to choose first. Instead he said to Lot, “Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:9). He gave up the advantage first and left the outcome to God.

Today, our “meat offered to idols” might be: which restaurant to choose for a team dinner, planning an outing in a group chat, who sits at the head table at a family gathering, parking spaces in the neighborhood, who steps into the elevator first. Every day brings dozens of small decisions, and in each one we can ask, “Who benefits from this choice?”

Paul’s overarching principle is: “Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Letting others benefit isn’t about being called a nice person; it’s about letting people glimpse what God is like in the small things. Today, pick one small decision and deliberately let someone else benefit first. You will discover that the moment you let go of yourself, your heart is actually free.
lessons.light: Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. It rarely happens in dramatic moments; it hides in the dozens of small choices we make every day. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means letting his will come first even in small things like eating and drinking.
think: In 1 Corinthians 10:31-33, what is Paul’s purpose in “not seeking my own profit”?
In what everyday matters do I unconsciously grab my own advantage first?
What small decision today can I deliberately use to let someone else benefit first?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving me every good thing first—even giving me your Son. In today’s small matters, teach me to ask “Who benefits?” and not only “What do I get?” In my eating and drinking and in every choice, let me glorify your name. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in one everyday decision (choosing a restaurant, waiting in line, dividing up tasks, picking seats), deliberately let a coworker, family member, or friend choose first—and don’t mention that you gave way.
lessons.quick: In every small decision, ask: “Who benefits from this choice?”
text: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are profitable. “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things build up.
Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.
Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Give no occasion for stumbling, whether to Jews, to Greeks, or to the assembly of God;
even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.

lessons.title: The Argument at the Last Supper
lessons.hear:
This is one of the most heartbreaking scenes in the Bible. Jesus had just instituted the Lord’s Supper, saying, “This is my body which is given for you.” And at that very table, “A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest” (Luke 22:24). The Lord was about to lay down his life for them, and they were comparing who was most important.

Don’t be too quick to blame the disciples, because we often do the same. On a church ministry team, we quietly compare whose ministry gets more attention. At a class reunion, within three sentences the talk turns to whose job is better and which school whose kids attend. In a group chat, it’s whose post gets more likes. Envy, bragging, and pride often hide in the most sacred settings. Ask yourself honestly: at which “table” this week was my heart measuring who is bigger?

Jesus didn’t respond with a scolding. He reminded them to look at him: “But I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). Then he spoke some deeply tender words to Peter. He knew Peter was about to deny him three times, yet he didn’t write that down against him in advance. Instead he said, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

This is what it means to take no account of evil. The Lord knows our failures, yet he doesn’t use them to condemn us; instead he prays for us and prepares our mission for after we turn back. The road to adjustment is this: when the urge to compare rises up, turn your eyes to the Lord who is “among you as one who serves”; when you want to dig up someone’s old wrongs, remember how the Lord doesn’t dig up ours.
lessons.light: Comparison is the thermometer of the self-centered life: the more we care about ourselves, the more we care about who is greater. Pride provokes pride, and everyone loses; humility inspires humility, and everyone wins. We review not to blame ourselves, but to “turn again” like Peter—and after turning, to strengthen others.
think: In Luke 22:24-32, how does Jesus respond to the disciples’ dispute and to Peter’s weakness?
In what setting this week was my heart also measuring myself against others?
What old wrong of someone else’s am I willing to hand over to the Lord today and stop digging up?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, while your disciples argued about who was greatest, you still served them; before Peter fell, you had already prayed for him. Forgive me for comparing and bragging among people, and forgive me for keeping a record of others’ wrongs. Help me turn again, and after turning, strengthen my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one “debt” or old grudge you’ve been holding on to. Pray for that person, then tear up the paper as a sign that you are handing the account over to the Lord.
lessons.quick: The Lord doesn’t dig up my old wrongs—he prays for me; so I will stop keeping score on others.
text: A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.
He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.
“But you are those who have continued with me in my trials.
I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me,
that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat,
but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”

lessons.title: Becoming a Rare Timothy
lessons.hear:
Writing to the church in Philippi from prison, Paul said he hoped to send Timothy to visit them, and explained why: “For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you. For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:20-21). These words are startling. Among the co-workers around Paul, someone who truly didn’t seek his own was that rare.

How did Timothy become like this? Paul says, “As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News” (Philippians 2:22). Timothy wasn’t born selfless; he learned it bit by bit as he followed Paul. He had seen Paul weep over the churches and keep caring for others even in prison. As he watched, he grew into the same likeness. Selfless love can be passed down.

This week we have seen that love is a string of “nots.” We have learned to bear the weaknesses of others, to seek others’ good in small things, and to turn back and look to the Lord when comparison rises up. These practices need repeating, because “seeking our own” is an old habit. But every time we choose to let someone else benefit first, the old self steps back and the new self grows a little.

Today, consider two things. First, who is your Paul? Who has shown you love that doesn’t seek its own? Go and thank them. Second, who might be your Timothy? Perhaps a younger coworker, a new small group member, or your own child. Invite them to join you in serving someone, and let them see how you put other people’s needs first. No need to lecture—just let them see it from beside you.
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children. The best way to pass on a selfless life is not to explain it, but to let people see it up close, the way Paul brought Timothy along. The secret of multiplication: first become that rare person, then walk with someone else until they become that rare person too.
think: In Philippians 2:19-22, how does Paul describe the difference between Timothy and others?
In my life, who has been a Paul who “didn’t seek his own”?
Which “Timothy” can I invite to join me in serving others?
lessons.speak: Lord, in a generation where everyone seeks their own, make me someone who truly cares about others. Thank you for placing selfless examples in my life. And let me bring a younger brother or sister alongside me, so that together we learn to seek the things of Jesus Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message thanking someone who showed you selfless love. Then invite a younger brother or sister to join you this week in visiting or helping someone.
lessons.quick: Everyone seeks their own; may I become a rare Timothy—and raise up the next one.
text: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.

weeks.title: Love Never Fails
weeks.theme: Gifts will cease and knowledge will pass away, but love carries eternal weight; the love we give today still counts in heaven tomorrow.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 13:7-13. According to Paul, what will be “done away with,” and what will “remain”?
Is there a relationship you’ve recently wanted to “give up on” or walk away from? What has worn you out?
This week, what is one thing you are willing to do to keep love going in a relationship that is growing cold?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, reach out to a friend or relative you were once close to but haven’t been in touch with for a long time, and set up a phone call or a meet-up. Before you go, pray, “Lord, your love never fails—please let our relationship grow warm again.” There’s no need to rush to explain the past; just greet them sincerely and listen to how they’re doing. Afterward, thank God for a friendship that continues in his hands.

lessons.title: Only Three Things Remain
lessons.hear:
Anyone who has moved house knows that packing is when you discover what really matters. At the end of 1 Corinthians 13, Paul does some “eternal packing” for us. He says prophecies, tongues, and knowledge will all be done away with, but “Love never fails” (1 Corinthians 13:8). In the end, “now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Why is love the greatest? Because in heaven, faith will become sight and hope will be fulfilled, but love will not end—it will be made complete. Right now “we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Every act of true love in our relationships today is not something that gets used up; it is something we can carry into eternity.

So what does never-failing love look like on earth? Paul says love “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7). To bear is to be like a roof, sheltering people from wind and rain. To believe is not to jump to the worst conclusion about people. To hope is to trust that God hasn’t finished writing this person’s story. To endure is to keep holding on while we wait.

A clear balance is needed here. “Believes all things” doesn’t mean being naïvely deceived, and “bears all things” doesn’t mean tolerating violence or abuse. Love rejoices with the truth, so when we face fraud, bullying, or abuse, safety and truth come first. Never-failing love does not mean never guarding yourself. It means that even when you need to step back, you keep praying for that person and leave their ending in God’s hands. Love can change its form without going out.
lessons.light: From the temporary to the eternal—this is the key shift in viewpoint in the 321 Vision. Seen with earthly eyes, relationships expire and gatherings break up. Seen with heavenly eyes, every true act of love helps build God’s system and lasts forever. When our focus is on Jesus, we can see eternal value in passing relationships.
think: In 1 Corinthians 13:8-13, what images does Paul use to contrast the “partial” with the “complete”?
Do I treat certain relationships as disposable, something I can throw away at any time?
Today, toward whom can I “hope all things,” and say something that shows I believe they can grow?
lessons.speak: Lord, your love never fails. I confess that my love often has an expiration date: when I’m hurt I take it back, and when I’m tired I let go. Put an eternal perspective in my heart, so that I know every act of true love today counts in heaven. And give me wisdom to hold on to truth and boundaries in love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you have “given up on” in your heart, and pray a “hopes all things” prayer for them. If appropriate, send them a sincere word of blessing.
lessons.quick: Knowledge will pass and gifts will cease, but love will be carried into eternity.
text: bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.
Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.
But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

lessons.title: Love Covers a Multitude of Sins
lessons.hear:
In a group chat of college friends going back twenty years, a sister was the target of a hurtful joke by an old classmate in front of everyone. The more she thought about it, the angrier she got. Her finger was already hovering over the “Leave Group” button. She thought, “Everyone’s busy anyway. One relationship less won’t make a difference.”

This is a very common old mindset in our day: relationships are disposable—stay if it works, leave if it doesn’t. One tap to block, one click to leave the group, quietly never getting in touch again—it all seems like the easiest way out. But if every offense makes us walk away, we will eventually find no one left around us, because sooner or later everyone will offend us, and we will offend others too.

Peter gives God’s point of view: “And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). These words echo Proverbs: “Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs” (Proverbs 10:12). Covering doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened. It means not magnifying someone’s fault, not spreading it around, and not letting it become the end of the relationship. Like a coat thrown over someone shivering in the cold, love chooses to protect rather than expose. Peter also says, “the end of all things is near” (1 Peter 4:7). Seen from eternity, many things that annoy us are not worth losing a relationship over.

That sister didn’t tap “Leave.” First she poured out her hurt to the Lord in prayer, and then she messaged the classmate privately: “What you said made me a bit sad. I don’t think you meant it that way.” He apologized immediately. Of course, love’s covering does not include hiding crimes or enabling harm. But for everyday offenses, love chooses to continue, not to cut off.
lessons.light: Self-centered relationships are transactions: when I’m shortchanged, I terminate the contract. Selfless love is a covenant: even when offended, it chooses to continue. Letting Jesus reign means letting his heart, not my emotions, decide whether a relationship stays or goes. Relationships matter more than things—and more than saving face.
think: In 1 Peter 4:7-11, how does “the end of all things is near” shape the way we love one another?
Have I recently felt the urge to block someone, leave a group, or cut off contact? Why?
In that relationship, how can I first “cover” rather than “expose”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, your love has covered my many sins; you did not publicly shame me for my faults. Forgive me for so often wanting to cut off a relationship over a small offense. Give me an eternal perspective, so that I love earnestly and cover others’ wrongs with love; and give me the courage to speak gently and clearly about the hurt in my heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If there is a relationship you want to “leave” today, pause before blocking or leaving any group. Pray for the other person, and then privately express your feelings in one gentle, specific sentence.
lessons.quick: An offense doesn’t have to be the end of a relationship; love chooses to cover and to continue.
text: But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.
And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Love in Deed and Truth
lessons.hear:
Never-failing love is not a long-lasting feeling; it is a sustained series of actions. Feelings rise and fall like ocean waves, but actions can be like a lighthouse, shining every day. John says, “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

We are all very good at loving in words: typing “You got this!” in a group chat, leaving a heart under a post, telling a sick friend, “Let me know if you need anything.” These are all good. But often what people really need is not “Let me know if you need anything,” because they are too exhausted even to ask. Love has to take one more step forward—from the tongue to the hands and feet.

John sets a very high standard: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16). We may not have to die for someone today, but we can lay down a little time, a little money, a little convenience. Choose one of these three directions and act on it:

1. Bring a meal: prepare dinner for a friend who has just had a baby, is sick, or is grieving, and drop it off at their door.
2. Keep company: go with an elderly person to a doctor’s appointment, or help a friend who just moved get to know the area.
3. Keep going: for someone in a long-term hardship, set a regular weekly check-in until they have come through it.

The third is the hardest, and the closest to “never fails.” Many people show up in the first few days of someone’s crisis, but few are still there in the third month. Never-failing love means you still remember when everyone else has forgotten.
lessons.light: A changed life changes the way we live. The life of love has to be worked out in the details of daily living, or it is just talk. The “2” in 920 is not a one-time list but relationships to be watered continually. “Do” is the last step of See · Hear · Think · Speak · Do, and it is where love becomes visible.
think: In 1 John 3:16-18, how does John move from the cross to everyday love?
Does my love often stop at “word” and “tongue”? When was the most recent time?
Who around me is in a long-term hardship, and how can I keep walking alongside them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you laid down your life for me and showed me what love is. Forgive me for so often loving only with my mouth, rarely with my hands, and rarely for the long haul. Today, help me carry love from my tongue to my hands and feet, to give real time and care to someone, and to keep remembering after others have forgotten. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one concrete thing for a friend going through a hard time (bring a meal, keep them company, run an errand), and set a weekly reminder on your phone to check in on them for a month.
lessons.quick: Many show up in the first few days; love still remembers in the third month.
text: By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.title: Leaving Your First Love
lessons.hear:
The church in Ephesus was an “excellent” church. The Lord commended their toil, their perseverance, and their discernment between true and false, and said they had endured for his name’s sake and had not grown weary. But then he said, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). The ministry was still running, but the love had gone cold.

This is a lot like some long-term relationships. Two old friends who now only exchange small talk when they meet. A ministry team that has served together for years and now only divides up tasks. A family group chat with nothing but forwarded posts and holiday stickers. On the surface everything looks normal, but inside the temperature has slowly dropped. Jesus foretold, “Because iniquity will be multiplied, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). Coldness usually doesn’t happen in a day; it happens gradually.

Take an honest look: Who did I once reach out to, but now I just wait for them to contact me? Which group of people did I once pray for, but now I treat them merely as colleagues? What made my love grow cold? Busyness, hurt, or the feeling that “they’ll never change anyway”?

The Lord’s correction has three very practical steps: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works” (Revelation 2:5). To remember is to recall why you loved this person in the first place. To repent is to admit that your love has gone cold and ask the Lord to rekindle it. To do the first works is to do again those simple acts of love from the early days—a phone call, a greeting, a meal. The warmth of love often returns the moment we start acting again.
lessons.light: When ministry replaces relationships, tasks have become more important than people. The 321 Vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The church in Ephesus had the order reversed. The road to adjustment is to come back from ministry to people, and from people back to the Lord who first loved us.
think: In Revelation 2:2-5, what did the Lord commend in the church in Ephesus, and what did he rebuke?
Toward whom has my love quietly “grown cold” without my noticing?
What specifically are the “first works” I will do again for that person?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you see my busyness and labor, and you also see my love slowly growing cold. I remember where I have fallen from, and I repent before you. Rekindle my first love, so that I am not just completing ministry tasks but truly loving every person you have entrusted to me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a friend, ministry partner, or family member toward whom your love has cooled, and do something you used to do often when your relationship began: call them, invite them for a meal, or write a few words of thanks.
lessons.quick: Remember, repent, do the first works; love’s warmth returns through action.
text: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: “He who holds the seven stars in his right hand, he who walks among the seven golden lamp stands says these things:
“I know your works, and your toil and perseverance, and that you can’t tolerate evil men, and have tested those who call themselves apostles, and they are not, and found them false.
You have perseverance and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not grown weary.
But I have this against you, that you left your first love.
Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works; or else I am coming to you swiftly, and will move your lamp stand out of its place, unless you repent.

lessons.title: You Are Our Glory and Joy
lessons.hear:
Paul stayed in Thessalonica only a short time before he was forced to leave. Yet he wrote that he had been “bereaved of you for a short season in presence, not in heart” (1 Thessalonians 2:17). Then he asked a beautiful question: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Isn’t it even you, before our Lord Jesus at his coming?” (1 Thessalonians 2:19)

Think about it: the crown Paul wanted to carry into eternity was not how many letters he had written or how many churches he had planted. It was faces, one after another. He saw people as his eternal joy. This is the most beautiful application of “love never fails”: the people we love today will be our joy and our crown on the day the Lord returns.

Over these four weeks we have walked through the life of love: God loved us first; love has two hands, patience and kindness; love doesn’t seek its own way; love never fails. These truths don’t end when we finish reading. We need to live them out again and again until they become our very nature. Starting next week, we will study the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, one fruit each week, and see how this love bears different kinds of fruit in our relationships.

Today, like Paul, speak what is in your heart to someone. Paul once wrote that “we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8). You don’t have to put it that strongly, but you can tell a spiritual companion, a small group member, or your child, “Thank you for being in my life. You are my joy.” It may sound ordinary, but they may remember it for the rest of their lives.
lessons.light: From earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal—Paul saw people with these eyes, so to him people were crowns, not tools. This is exactly the perspective that builds God’s system. Multiplication is not copying activities; it is helping more people stand before the Lord and become our eternal joy.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 2:17-20, what does Paul regard as his crown and joy?
Over these four weeks on the life of love, which truth has changed me most?
To whom will I say, “You are my joy”? What is the most sincere way to say it?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for leading me these four weeks into the life of love. Your love never fails, and it lets me see eternal value in people. May the people I love be found standing before you when you come, as my joy and crown. And help me put this love into words today. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write a few lines to a spiritual companion, small group member, or family member, telling them specifically what they mean in your life. End with: “You are my joy.”
lessons.quick: Paul’s crown was not his achievements but faces—people standing before the Lord.
text: But we, brothers, being bereaved of you for a short season in presence, not in heart, tried even harder to see your face with great desire,
because we wanted to come to you—indeed, I, Paul, once and again—but Satan hindered us.
For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Isn’t it even you, before our Lord Jesus at his coming?
For you are our glory and our joy.

weeks.keyText: Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.

weeks.title: Love: Your Neighbor as Yourself
weeks.theme: Loving our neighbor as ourselves means first giving the people around us the kindness we ourselves long for.
group: Read Matthew 22:34-40. Why does Jesus answer by putting “love God” and “love your neighbor” together?
Can you give an example of whether you usually ask “Who is my neighbor?” or “Whose neighbor am I willing to become?”
This week, which neighbor will you treat first in the way you most long to be treated?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, do a “Good Samaritan” act for a neighbor in your community who gets little attention: buy groceries for an elderly person living alone, show a newly arrived family the nearby market and clinic, or invite them over for tea. Before you go, pray and ask the Lord to show you their real needs. If the person is of the opposite sex or someone you don’t know well, invite a family member or friend to come along. When you get home, give thanks and pray for this new “2” in your life.

lessons.title: Two Commandments, One Heart
lessons.hear:
Starting this week, we will study one fruit each week from this list: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). These nine are not nine different bunches of fruit; they are like the nine segments of a single orange, all belonging to one life—the life of Christ. The first segment is love.

A lawyer asked Jesus, “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?” Jesus answered with the first: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind. But he didn’t stop there. He went on to add a second: “A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Matthew 22:39). He said, “The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments” (Matthew 22:40). The entire Old Testament is like a painting hanging on these two nails.

The word “likewise” matters. Loving people is not a separate subject apart from loving God; it is the natural extension of loving God. Think of a tree: its roots go down deep into God’s love, and its branches reach out toward people. Someone who says he loves God but is cold toward the people around him is like a tree that claims to have deep roots but never grows a single leaf.

So what does “as yourself” mean? It doesn’t mean we must first learn to love ourselves before we can love others. It means that you already take care of yourself quite naturally—you eat when you’re hungry, put on a coat when you’re cold, and hope someone will care when you’re hurt. Paul says, “no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5:29). Loving your neighbor as yourself means treating others with that same natural, attentive care. However you would cherish yourself, cherish them that way.
lessons.light: In 920, the “9” is the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, and the first of these is love; the “2” is everyone I am in relationship with; the “0” is selflessness. Loving our neighbor as ourselves is exactly letting the “0” become the channel that carries the “9” to the “2.” The order of relationships is God first, then people—which is why the second commandment always follows right behind the first.
think: In Matthew 22:37-40, how does Jesus connect loving God with loving people?
How big is the gap between how attentively I care for myself and how attentively I care for others?
Today, whom can I cherish in the same way I cherish myself?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me first, so that I can love you with all my heart, soul, and mind. Let my love for you flow naturally to the people around me. I know very well how to care for myself, yet I often overlook others’ needs. Holy Spirit, produce the fruit of love in me, so that I love my neighbor as myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think about how you most want to be treated when you are tired, sick, or sad. Then find someone who is in that state right now and treat them that way.
lessons.quick: Loving God is the root, loving people is the branch; the two commandments are one life.
text: But the Pharisees, when they heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered themselves together.
One of them, a lawyer, asked him a question, testing him.
“Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?”
Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’
This is the first and great commandment.
A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.”

lessons.title: Go and Be a Neighbor
lessons.hear:
A brother working in Singapore walked past the office pantry every day and saw a foreign cleaning lady there.
