He always gave a nod and kept going, thinking, “She’s not my colleague, and she’s not my friend.” Then one day he saw her sitting in the stairwell, quietly wiping away tears. In that moment, he remembered the parable of the Good Samaritan.

The lawyer asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” What he wanted was a boundary line: which people I must love, and which people I can ignore. This is our old mindset too—a neighbor is a “circle”: my family, my friends, my church, my community. People outside the circle have nothing to do with me.

But Jesus didn’t answer “who is.” He told a story and then turned the question around: “Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” (Luke 10:36). He flipped the question: a neighbor is not a circle I get to filter; it is an identity I choose to take on. The priest and the Levite both “passed by on the other side.” They had their status and their reasons. But the Samaritan “was moved with compassion.” He stopped, came close, bandaged the wounds, paid the bill, and even promised to come back.

That day, the brother did not pass by on the other side. He sat down and asked the cleaning lady what was wrong, and learned that her child back home was sick but she had been too afraid to ask for time off. He prayed with her, and later gathered a few coworkers to put together a small gift. He said, “I thought I was helping her, but actually God was teaching me what it means to love my neighbor as myself.” Jesus’ final words speak to us as well: “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:37).
lessons.light: The self-centered person asks, “Who deserves my love?” The selfless person asks, “Whose neighbor can I become?” The first draws boundaries; the second crosses them. From a human point of view to God’s point of view: God crossed the greatest distance of all, from heaven, to become our neighbor—so we have the strength to cross the invisible lines around us.
think: In Luke 10:31-34, how do the responses of the priest, the Levite, and the Samaritan differ?
How big is the “neighbor circle” in my heart, and who is often left outside it?
Today, whom can I stop for and become a neighbor to, instead of “passing by on the other side”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you came from heaven to my side, became my neighbor, and bound up my wounds. Forgive me for so often drawing lines, loving only the people in my circle and passing by everyone else on the other side. Move me with compassion, so that I stop, come close to someone in need, and go and do likewise. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, notice someone you pass every day but have never really greeted (a cleaner, a building manager, a shop clerk). Stop, call them by name or ask their name, greet them, and remember it.
lessons.quick: A neighbor is not a circle I filter, but an identity I choose to take on.
text: But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?”
Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.title: As You Would Want to Be Treated
lessons.hear:
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus gave a standard of love that anyone can understand: “Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them” (Matthew 7:12). Many cultures have a similar saying, such as Confucius’ “Do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself.” But Jesus goes a step further. It’s not only “don’t do” what others dislike; it’s “take the initiative to do” what you yourself would want others to do. One is holding back from harm; the other is actively reaching out in love.

Notice the first word of that sentence: “Therefore.” It connects to what came just before—how the Father gives good things to his children who ask him. Jesus says, “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11). We can take the initiative to treat others well because the Father first took the initiative to treat us well. The power to love our neighbor as ourselves doesn’t come from moral pressure; it comes from gratitude for the Father’s generous kindness.

Today, let’s turn this standard into a very concrete exercise. Open the notes app on your phone and write down three things you most wish others would do for you. For example: “I wish someone would remember my birthday.” “I wish someone had shown me around when I was new.” “I wish that when I make a mistake, someone would tell me privately instead of calling me out in the group chat.”

Then choose one of the three and do it for someone today. Maybe it’s remembering a coworker’s birthday, taking a new small group member out to lunch, or turning a public reply full of criticism into a private message. You’ll discover that the best textbook for loving your neighbor as yourself is hidden in your own longings.
lessons.light: Change begins with me: don’t wait for others to be good to me first; I will be good to them first. This is the initiative of selflessness—not because the other person deserves it, but because the Father has first been generous to me. See · Hear · Think · Speak · Do: “Think” about what you long for, then “Do” it for others first.
think: In Matthew 7:11-12, the word “Therefore” links the Father’s generosity to how we treat others. What does this show us?
How do I most want others to treat me, and do I treat others that way myself?
Today, which “way I long to be treated” will I give to someone first, and to whom?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you have never been stingy in giving me good things. Thank you for being so generous and taking the initiative to bless me. Help me stop waiting for others to be good to me first, and instead treat the people around me the way I long to be treated. Today, let me do for someone what I also long to have done for me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three things you most wish others would do for you. Pick one and do it today for a coworker, classmate, or neighbor.
lessons.quick: The way you most long to be treated is your textbook for how to treat others today.
text: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
Or who is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.

lessons.title: The Opposite of Loving Your Neighbor
lessons.hear:
Many people don’t realize that “love your neighbor as yourself” first appears not in the New Testament but in Leviticus. And its context is remarkably down-to-earth: “You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people” (Leviticus 19:16); “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Leviticus 19:17); and only then: “You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

This passage is like a mirror that shows us the opposite of loving our neighbor as ourselves:

1. Slander: forwarding someone’s private business in a group chat, gossiping over dinner about someone who isn’t there.
2. Hatred in the heart: polite on the surface, but nursing a grudge inside, so that nothing the other person says sits right with you.
3. Vengeance and grudges: not necessarily anything dramatic—maybe just deliberately not replying to messages, leaving someone off the invitation list, or sneering behind their back.

Take an honest look: this week, did I talk about someone who wasn’t present, in some group chat or gathering? Is there someone in my heart I’m polite to but don’t love? In Scripture, Miriam once spoke against Moses behind his back, and she was struck with leprosy. But Moses did not take revenge; instead he cried out to God to heal her (see Numbers 12:1-13). This is a beautiful picture of how love sets things right: the one who was talked about responds with prayer, and the one who did the talking is healed in grace.

Leviticus also gives a positive path: “You shall surely rebuke your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:17). If there’s a problem, speak to the person directly and gently, not behind their back. Sometimes loving your neighbor as yourself means having the courage to tell the truth to someone’s face instead of gossiping behind their back.
lessons.light: The self-centered heart finds it easiest to talk behind people’s backs, because pointing out others’ faults makes us look better. The selfless heart doesn’t need to put others down to lift itself up. Each evening, using the three questions of the app’s Word Watch to examine yourself is a good habit for keeping slander outside the door.
think: In Leviticus 19:15-18, what behaviors are set in opposition to “love your neighbor as yourself”?
This week, did I talk behind the back of someone who wasn’t present? What did I say?
Toward the person I’ve been holding a grudge against, how will I shift to direct and gentle communication?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often gossip about people behind their backs and hold grudges while staying polite on the surface. Forgive me, and cleanse my lips and my thoughts. Give me the courage to speak the truth gently to people’s faces, and the grace to stop spreading slander and instead love my neighbor as myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, if someone in a group chat or gathering starts discussing the private affairs of someone not present, gently change the subject. If you yourself have done this, confess it privately to the Lord, and if needed, apologize to the person.
lessons.quick: The opposite of loving your neighbor is often one bit of gossip behind their back.
text: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
“‘You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people. “‘You shall not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am the LORD.
“‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.
“‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.

lessons.title: The Debt of Love We Never Finish Paying
lessons.hear:
Chinese culture places great weight on “owing favors.” When we owe someone a favor, we feel uneasy until we find a chance to pay it back. Paul says something remarkable: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8). Every other debt should be paid off, but the debt of love is never finished—and we should gladly keep owing it.

Why? Because we have received so much love from Christ that we could never repay it in a lifetime. We can’t pay him back directly, yet he tells us: pay this love forward to the people around you. So loving people is not an extra good deed; it is paying down a debt we will never finish paying. Paul goes on: “Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10).

This week we have seen that loving God and loving people are one life. We have learned to take the initiative to become someone’s neighbor, to treat others the way we long to be treated, and to examine the opposite of love—gossip behind people’s backs. These lessons need repeating, because love is not a one-time act but a fruit tree that must bear fruit season after season.

Today, pass this idea of the “debt of love” on to someone. You could sit down with a small group member or your child and list together “whose love we owe”: who has cared for us, prayed for us, helped us when things were hard. Then choose one person together, and use this week’s practices to “pay back” a little love. When you bring someone else along to love, the fruit of love begins to grow on another tree.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 is not just my list of contacts; it is the people to whom I owe love. Every face is an opportunity God gives me to pay down my debt of love. Multiplication means bringing someone else along to love, so that love bears fruit from one tree to the next, building a network of relationships that belongs to God.
think: In Romans 13:8-10, how does Paul say all the commandments are “summed up” in loving your neighbor as yourself?
At what moment this week did I most genuinely “pay back” a little of my debt of love?
Whom will I bring along with me to pay a debt of love, and toward whom?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I owe you a love I could never repay in a lifetime. Thank you for letting me pay that love forward to the people around me. Keep me always aware of what I owe, loving without keeping score and without stopping; and let me bring a brother or sister along with me to love the people you have placed around us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in the app’s 920 Relationship Map, add a card for someone you “owe a debt of love” and write a prayer for them. Then invite a small group member or family member to do one act of love for that person with you this week.
lessons.quick: Other debts should be paid off, but the debt of love is never finished—so gladly keep owing it, and keep loving.
text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.

weeks.keyText: A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’

weeks.title: Joy: Rejoicing with Those Who Rejoice
weeks.theme: Genuinely celebrating other people’s good news is a mark of selflessness—and joy that is shared comes back doubled.
group: Read Romans 12:9-16. What concrete expressions of “love without hypocrisy” does Paul describe?
Which is harder for you: weeping with those who weep, or rejoicing with those who rejoice? Why?
This week, which friend’s good news will you celebrate with them in a concrete way?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, throw a small celebration for a friend who recently had good news (getting into school, landing a job, a new baby, recovering from illness, being baptized): a bouquet of flowers, a cake, or a meal with a few friends to bless them. Before you go, pray that the Lord would make your joy genuine; during the gathering, invite everyone to pray with thanksgiving for them. When you get home, thank God that you were able to rejoice with someone else.

lessons.title: Let Love Be Without Hypocrisy
lessons.hear:
The second fruit of the Spirit is joy. Joy is not just a personal good mood; in relationships it takes a very concrete shape: “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). This is our memory verse for the week.

People often observe that weeping with those who weep is actually easier than rejoicing with those who rejoice. When a friend runs into trouble, sympathy comes naturally. But when a friend gets promoted, gets married, has a child accepted into a top school, or buys a new home, our congratulations often carry a slightly sour taste. Other people’s tears don’t threaten me, but other people’s joy can make me feel I’ve fallen behind. So truly rejoicing with those who rejoice often takes more selflessness than weeping with them.

Paul places this line within a whole passage describing love, and the first sentence is: “Let love be without hypocrisy” (Romans 12:9). Hypocritical rejoicing says “Congratulations!” with the lips while comparing in the heart; it clicks “like” in the group chat and then privately tells others, “He just got lucky.” Genuine rejoicing treats someone else’s good news as if it happened in your own family.

Where does joy come from? Paul speaks of “rejoicing in hope” (Romans 12:12). The Old Testament says, “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10). When someone has a source of joy in God, they don’t need to beat others in order to be happy. Their cup is already full, so they can be glad when someone else’s cup is full too. This kind of joy is contagious in relationships. It is like one lamp lighting another: its own light isn’t diminished one bit.
lessons.light: The self-centered person treats others’ joy as their own loss; the selfless person treats others’ joy as their own gift. Within the “9” of 920, joy follows right behind love—because only a heart that loves people can truly rejoice for them. When our focus is on Jesus, we don’t have to look for our own place in other people’s achievements.
think: In Romans 12:9-16, which phrases relate to being “of the same mind” and not comparing?
The last time I heard a friend’s good news, what was my first reaction inside?
Today, how can I sincerely rejoice over someone’s good news?
lessons.speak: Lord, you are the source of my joy. Forgive me for feeling sour when others are blessed, and for saying congratulations without meaning it. Make my love genuine, without hypocrisy. Let my cup overflow in you, so that I can truly rejoice over others’ good news and also weep with those who weep. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a friend who recently had good news and tell them specifically, “I’m so happy for you, because …”—naming the effort or grace you see behind their good news.
lessons.quick: Others’ tears test my compassion; others’ joy tests my selflessness.
text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.

lessons.title: Rejoice with Me
lessons.hear:
A sister in her thirties, still waiting and praying for marriage, saw in her college group chat that a close friend had announced her engagement. Under the message came a long line of “Congratulations!”—but she couldn’t bring herself to type anything. In her heart she said, “Why her again? I’ve prayed for so many years.” In the end she put her phone face down and pretended she hadn’t seen it.

This is a very real struggle, and it reveals an old mindset: someone else’s gain is my loss. As if life were one big cake, and if someone takes an extra slice, there’s less for me. Under this mindset, a friend’s happy news becomes a reminder to me—a reminder that I don’t have it yet, I’m not enough, I’m behind.

In Luke 15, Jesus told two parables that show us heaven’s point of view. The shepherd finds his lost sheep, the woman finds her lost coin, and the first thing each of them does is the same: “he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’” (Luke 15:6). Heaven’s joy is never kept to oneself; it invites the neighbors to share in it. In God’s kingdom, joy is not a limited cake but a spring that grows the more it is shared.

Later, that sister honestly poured out her pain to the Lord, and she found that God didn’t rebuke her; he comforted her. A few days later, she called her friend and said, “I’m really happy for you, and I’d love to help you get ready for the wedding.” She said that in that moment the bitterness in her heart didn’t disappear, but something sweet from God was added to it. Rejoicing with others doesn’t require us to pretend we have no pain. When we hand our pain to the Lord, our hands are freed to take hold of someone else’s joy.
lessons.light: From an earthly point of view, joy is scarce; from heaven’s point of view, joy is abundant. Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset. Letting Jesus reign means trusting that he has a good timetable for my life too, so I don’t have to compete with others or feel deflated when they are blessed.
think: In the two parables of Luke 15:3-10, what does each person do after finding what was lost?
Do I also carry the idea that “someone else’s gain is my loss”? In what area?
About the good news that leaves me feeling sour, how will I first be honest with the Lord and then go and bless?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, joy in your kingdom is abundant and never runs short. I confess that I often treat others’ good news as my own loss, feeling sour and avoiding them. I hand you my disappointment and my waiting; please comfort me. And free my hands to rejoice sincerely with those who rejoice. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a piece of good news that leaves you feeling sour. Today, first tell the Lord honestly how you feel, and then take the initiative to send that person a sincere blessing—without any comparison attached.
lessons.quick: Heaven’s joy isn’t a limited cake but a spring that grows the more it’s shared.
text: He told them this parable:
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
“Or what woman, if she had ten drachma coins, if she lost one drachma coin, wouldn’t light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she found it?
When she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost!’
Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting.”

lessons.title: I Thank God Whenever I Remember You
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote Philippians, he was locked up in prison. By rights, he had every reason to write a letter full of complaints, yet this letter is known as “the epistle of joy.” He opens by saying, “I thank my God whenever I remember you, always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy” (Philippians 1:3-4).

Paul’s joy had a very important source: people. When he thought of the brothers and sisters in Philippi and how they had partnered with him in advancing the gospel, his heart was filled with joy. He even said, “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). He rejoiced not because his circumstances were good, but because he saw God at work in other people.

This is the kind of joy we can practice today: seeing God’s work in people, and then saying so. We often keep our gratitude in our hearts and rarely say it out loud; Chinese culture especially is not used to expressing appreciation directly. But one specific word of appreciation can give someone strength for days.

Today’s action is simple, but it takes a little courage:

1. Think of three people, and thank God for one good thing in each of them.
2. Choose one of them, and send a message or write a card telling them specifically, “I thank God whenever I think of you, because …”
3. Pray for one thing for them, and tell them in your message what you prayed.

You will find that when you speak your thanks aloud, joy doesn’t just reach the other person; it comes back into your own heart. Joy is like an echo: the more sincerely you call out, the louder it comes back.
lessons.light: Giving thanks in everything is the “God” of the Way of Service—all glory to God. Gratitude is the doorway to joy: when we see grace in others, our focus shifts away from ourselves. Among See · Hear · Think · Speak · Do, “Speak” is often neglected; saying thank you aloud is the first step to getting joy flowing.
think: In Philippians 1:3-8, what emotions fill Paul’s heart when he remembers the believers?
When was the last time I told someone specifically, “I thank God for you”?
Today, to whom will I put into words the work of God I see in them?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for placing so many wonderful people in my life—yet I rarely thank you for them, and even more rarely tell them. Today, open my eyes to see your good work in them, and open my mouth to speak my thanks aloud, so that joy flows among us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to a friend, ministry partner, or family member: “I thank God whenever I think of you, because …” Name one specific thing, and tell them what you prayed for them.
lessons.quick: See God’s work in people and say it out loud—and joy begins to flow.
text: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

It is even right for me to think this way on behalf of all of you, because I have you in my heart, because both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Good News, you all are partakers with me of grace.
For God is my witness, how I long after all of you in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: Saul’s Jealous Eye and John’s Joy
lessons.hear:
The Bible shows us two men who faced the same kind of situation yet responded in completely different ways. The first is King Saul. After David defeated Goliath, the women sang, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). Saul was deeply displeased, and Scripture says, “Saul watched David from that day and forward” (1 Samuel 18:9)—with a jealous, suspicious eye. From then on, someone else’s success became a thorn in his heart, right to the end of his life.

The second is John the Baptist. His disciples came to him anxiously and reported, “he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26). In effect they were saying, “Teacher, he’s stealing your following!” But John replied, “the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full” (John 3:29). Then he spoke those famous words: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Take an honest look: am I more like Saul or like John? When a coworker is praised by the boss, when another leader’s small group grows, when a friend’s post gets lots of responses, what is my first thought? “Why not me?” or “Thank you, Lord”? Envy is often not some huge sin but a small jealous look—a glance, a cool reply, a deliberate decision not to click “like.”

John’s secret is in verse 27: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” (John 3:27). He knew that everyone’s gifts and position come from God, so he didn’t need to grab for them. The way to adjust is to bring the person I envy before God, admit that everything is his gift, and learn to say with John, “He must increase.”
lessons.light: Saul left his proper place and treated someone else’s success as a threat to his throne; John kept to his proper place, knowing he was “the friend of the bridegroom.” Humility is returning to our proper place and letting God be God. When I know who I am, I don’t need to fear someone being greater than me—and that is the freedom of joy.
think: In John 3:26-30, how does John see his own role, and how does that bring him joy?
Whose success has recently made me uncomfortable? What small “jealous looks” have I given?
How will I pray for that person, and learn to say, “He must increase”?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that there is a jealous eye like Saul’s in my heart, and I feel threatened when others are blessed. Thank you for reminding me that everything is given from heaven. Help me keep to my proper place like John, and rejoice when others flourish. Today I bring to you the person I envy, and I ask you to bless them richly. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray specifically for God to bless the work, family, and faith of someone you feel a little envious of. If you have the chance, sincerely praise them for something they did well.
lessons.quick: Saul’s jealous eye cost him his joy; John said, “He must increase,” and his joy was made full.
text: They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.

lessons.title: No Greater Joy Than This
lessons.hear:
Late in life, the apostle John wrote a very short letter to a brother named Gaius. Brief as it is, it reveals the greatest joy in an old pastor’s heart: “I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth” (3 John 4).

John had experienced so much in his lifetime: walking with Jesus, seeing miracles, witnessing the resurrection, being exiled to an island. Yet in old age, he said his greatest joy was not his own experiences, but seeing his spiritual children grow in the truth. This is joy at its most mature: moving from “How am I doing?” to “How are you doing?”; from my own achievements to someone else’s growth. This is the summit of rejoicing with those who rejoice—even treating someone else’s growth as your own greatest joy.

This week we have learned the fruit of joy: love must be without hypocrisy; joy is not a limited cake; gratitude should be spoken aloud; and we can turn from Saul’s jealous eye to John’s “He must increase.” These practices need repeating, because comparison creeps back so easily. Every time someone else has good news, we get another chance to practice rejoicing with them.

Today, pass this joy on. Think of someone you have walked alongside, led, or taught—perhaps a small group member, a younger student, a friend who has just come to faith, or your own child. When you see even a little growth in them, tell them specifically, “I’ve seen how you’ve changed in this area, and it brings me real joy.” Growth that is noticed keeps growing—and you will discover that rejoicing in others’ growth is a joy that multiplies the more it is shared.
lessons.light: The “3” in 235: the greatest joy of spiritual parents is seeing their spiritual children walking in truth. The multiplication of joy is building our own joy on other people’s growth. Joy like this cannot be stolen by comparison, because at its root it is selfless.
think: In 3 John 1-4, what is John’s greatest joy, and what does that reveal about where his heart was?
This week, in what moment of sincerely rejoicing with someone did I experience joy being doubled?
Which person I have walked alongside will I affirm, and what specific growth will I name?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching me this week to rejoice with those who rejoice. Let my joy care less and less about my own achievements and more and more about others’ growth. I bring before you the people I have walked alongside—let them walk in truth, and help me to notice and speak of the changes in them often. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to someone you have walked alongside or led. Name one specific way you have seen them grow, and tell them, “I feel such joy because of you.”
lessons.quick: The most mature joy is seeing others walk in truth.
text: The elder to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth.
Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers.
For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth.
I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.

weeks.keyText: Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

weeks.title: Peace: Blessed Are the Peacemakers
weeks.theme: Peace is not pretending nothing happened; it is stepping into the breach and going first to be reconciled.
group: Read James 3:17-18. Why is the wisdom from above “first pure, then peaceful”?
What is your go-to way of “pretending nothing happened”? What are you afraid of losing?
Toward whom are you willing to take one step of peace this week, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a friend or relative with whom there’s been some tension—but who is still willing to meet—for a cup of tea or a simple meal. Before you go, pray for them and for yourself, asking the Lord for a gentle heart. When you meet, ask more questions and listen more; don’t rush to reopen old accounts. If the past involved real harm or safety concerns, talk with someone you trust first. Afterward, whatever the outcome, thank God for the step you took.

lessons.title: Blessed Are the Peacemakers
lessons.hear:
When Jesus preached the Beatitudes on the mountain, He said something remarkable: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). He didn’t say “blessed are the peace-lovers,” but “the peacemakers.” Peace-lovers may simply dislike arguments and take the long way around whenever conflict shows up. Peacemakers roll up their sleeves, step into the breach, and start repairing relationships that have already cracked. The first is like someone afraid of water standing on the shore; the second is like a levee worker who wades in, knowing full well he’s going to get wet.

Why will such people “be called children of God”? Because this is the very nature of the Father. The rift between God and humanity was not repaired by us; God sent His Son to come in Himself and close the breach with the cross. So when we work to mend relationships, we start to resemble our Father—people look at us and recognize the family likeness of God’s household.

James tells us where this kind of peace comes from: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy” (James 3:17). Notice the order: first pure, then peaceful. Real peace doesn’t sweep problems under the rug. First the heart is made clean before God, laying down bitter jealousy and selfish ambition; only then do we have the strength to reconcile. Earthly wisdom says, “Whoever apologizes first loses.” The wisdom from above says, “To lose to love is to win.”

James goes on: “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3:18). Peace is like a garden; it doesn’t grow overnight. Every gentle word, every time you bow your head first, every piece of gossip you refuse to pass on is a seed sown in the ground. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to the patch of ground near you that is waiting for the seed of peace.
lessons.light: In conflict, the self-centered person asks only, “Who’s right and who’s wrong?” The selfless person asks, “How can this relationship be healed?” Peacemaking is fruit the Holy Spirit bears in our relationships, and it is the work of building God’s system on earth: wherever someone is willing to lay down their pride, God’s kingdom comes one inch closer.
think: In James 3:13-18, what marks earthly wisdom, and what marks the wisdom from above?
When conflict comes, am I more like the one standing on the shore or the one wading in to repair the levee?
Which relationship around me needs me to sow a seed of peace today?
lessons.speak: Father, You sent Your Son into the breach between You and me and reconciled me to Yourself. Give me the wisdom from above: first cleanse my heart of bitterness and rivalry, then make me a peacemaker, so that people can see Your family likeness in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone with whom things feel a bit stiff (a coworker, a relative, or someone in a group chat). Pray for them once, and send them a simple message of greeting that has nothing to do with who was right.
lessons.quick: Peace-lovers avoid conflict; peacemakers step into the breach.
text: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.
But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth.
This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

lessons.title: Peace Isn’t Pretending
lessons.hear:
A sister who was well-liked in her extended family’s group chat dreaded Chinese New Year more than anything. Three years earlier, she and her cousin had argued over how to split an elderly relative’s medical bills. Since then they still “liked” each other’s posts in the group chat and still sat at the same table for the New Year dinner—they just never spoke one-on-one again. Relatives would say, “Haven’t you two gotten past that?” She told herself the same thing. Yet every time her cousin opened his mouth, her stomach tightened.

We often carry an old mindset: peace means not fighting; if we’re polite on the surface, we’re at peace. The best approach is to “give it the cold shoulder” and let time heal everything. But God sees it differently. Jesus said, “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23-24).

Notice that this isn’t “you have something against your brother,” but “your brother has anything against you.” Jesus wants us to care not only about the discomfort in our own hearts but also about the hurt in the other person’s heart—and it is so urgent that even worship can be put on hold. To God, relationships matter more than rituals, and people matter more than things. The cold shoulder is like putting a pretty bandage on a wound: nothing shows on the outside, but underneath it slowly festers.

Later, in her small group, that sister was moved by this passage. She didn’t bring it up publicly in the group chat. Instead, she invited her cousin out for coffee, and the first thing she said was, “I was too harsh that time. I’m sorry.” He froze for a moment, then his eyes welled up: “Actually, it’s been weighing on me too.” They never fully agreed on how to divide those medical bills, but the two of them could finally talk again. Peace doesn’t always mean every problem is solved; it means we’re willing to face it together.
lessons.light: Pretending nothing happened is a self-centered peace: it saves face and avoids discomfort while the relationship slowly dies. A selfless peace is willing to bow first and speak first, because the focus isn’t on my face but on the fact that the other person is one of my “2”—someone God has placed in my life for me to love. People matter more than things; relationships matter more than face.
think: In Matthew 5:23-24, what does Jesus tell us to stop, and what does He tell us to do first?
Do I have a relationship that looks polite on the surface but has long since frozen over?
How could I take the first step toward reconciliation with that person?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often use politeness to cover wounds and the cold shoulder in place of reconciliation. I bring my gift before You while there is still someone I haven’t made peace with. Give me courage to go first and humility to say “I’m sorry” first, and prepare that person’s heart as well. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of someone with whom things look fine on the surface but there’s still a knot. Pray for them first, then think of one sincere sentence you could open with, and look for a chance to say it this week.
lessons.quick: The cold shoulder only bandages; reconciliation heals.
text: “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there until you have paid the last penny.

lessons.title: At Peace with All, as Far as It Depends on You
lessons.hear:
Paul gives us a very practical word: “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). The sentence has two halves, and we need to hear both. “As much as it is up to you” means peace isn’t a matter of mood; it calls for our full effort. “If it is possible” means peace takes two, and I can only be responsible for my side.

What can I do on my side? Paul goes on to say we should not repay evil for evil but leave room for God, and even, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Romans 12:20). The last line sums it all up: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). Evil spreads like an epidemic: you say one harsh word to me, and I fire back two; you leave my message on “read” in the group chat, so I gossip about you behind your back. People who repay evil with evil think they’re fighting back, but they’ve already been defeated by evil—they have taken on its shape. To overcome evil with good is to refuse the infection and then hand out the cure in the middle of the outbreak.

How can you practice this today? Here are three small steps. First, pause: when a message makes you angry, don’t reply right away. Take a deep breath and pray one sentence for the other person. Second, give way: on small matters that don’t touch truth or safety—where to eat, who pays for parking, who gets the final say in the group chat—let it go first. Third, send something good: take the initiative to do a small thing the other person can use, like saving a document for them or lending a hand when they’re busy.

At the same time, remember that “if it is possible” also protects you. If someone keeps humiliating, threatening, harassing, or deceiving you, being at peace doesn’t mean letting them hurt you. Keeping your distance, bringing along someone you trust, and when necessary seeking professional or legal help do not contradict this passage. Children of peace are not naïve; they are clear-eyed before God and refuse to let evil rule.
lessons.light: Repaying evil for evil is pride provoking pride, and everyone loses. Overcoming evil with good is humility drawing out humility, and everyone wins. Giving way is not weakness; it hands the right to avenge back to God. When I let God be God, I no longer have to play judge—I only need to do my part, on my side, as someone who works hard for peace.
think: In Romans 12:17-21, what things does Paul list that I can do “on my side”?
Whose recent words or actions have made me want to hit back?
What specific good thing can I send that person’s way today?
lessons.speak: Father, You say vengeance belongs to You, and I am willing to hand over the injustice I feel. Keep me from being overcome by evil. Help me pause when I want to snap back, give way on small things, and find strength to do one good thing for the person who wronged me. And give me wisdom to know when I need to protect myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one specific, small kindness for someone who has recently made you uncomfortable: forward them a useful piece of information, help them with a small task, or sincerely affirm them once in the group chat.
lessons.quick: Whoever repays evil with evil has already been defeated by evil.
text: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

lessons.title: When Paul and Barnabas Disagreed
lessons.hear:
You might assume great apostles never argue. But Luke honestly records that Paul and Barnabas disagreed about whether to take Mark along, and “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39). One was the “Son of Encouragement,” who had once risked his reputation to bring the newly converted Paul into the church; the other was the apostle to the Gentiles. Both loved the Lord and both carried a burden, yet they parted ways because they saw one person differently.

This passage is a mirror. Conflict often isn’t one good person against one bad person; it’s two good people each holding part of the truth. Paul valued the mission and feared that someone who had quit halfway would hold back the gospel. Barnabas valued the person and was willing to give someone who had fallen a second chance. When we see only our own half of the truth, it is easy to turn “I disagree with you” into “I don’t want you.” Ask yourself: in my most recent argument, did I also see only my half?

The good news is that the story doesn’t end with the split. Years later, writing to Timothy from prison, Paul said, “Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The man he once turned away became a helper in his later years. We don’t know what happened in between, but we know this: God gave up on no one, and time and grace slowly closed the breach.

The path of adjustment has three steps. First, admit it: my position may have merit, but my attitude may not have had love. Second, separation is not severance: sometimes people serve in different ways and can walk different roads for a season, but don’t pass a death sentence on the other person in your heart, and don’t list their faults in front of others. Third, leave a door open for restoration: pray for them regularly, and when the time is right, speak words of affirmation as Paul did.
lessons.light: The self-centered life turns “I disagree with you” into “I don’t want you”; the selfless life can still honor people in disagreement. Reconciliation sometimes takes time, and may even need a third party’s help, but the door must stay open. The focus is on Jesus, not on who’s right; where Jesus reigns, roads that parted can meet again.
think: In Acts 15:36-41, what did Paul care about, and what did Barnabas care about?
In my most recent conflict, which half of the truth was the other person holding?
For which broken relationship can I “leave a door open”? How?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You see how in arguments I cling to my half of the truth and turn disagreement into rejection. Forgive my pride. I place that broken relationship in Your hands. Keep me from condemning anyone in my heart, and in Your time, open a road to reconciliation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you drifted from after a disagreement. Tell a mutual friend one of their strengths, or send them a sincere word of affirmation directly.
lessons.quick: Conflict is often two good people each holding half the truth; reconciliation starts by seeing the other half.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

lessons.title: Follow After Peace, Uproot Bitterness
lessons.hear:
The writer of Hebrews uses a strong verb: “Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). To “follow after” here is the way a hunter chases his prey or a runner races for the finish line. Peace won’t just fall into your lap; you have to go after it.

Then he says, “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it” (Hebrews 12:15). Bitterness is like the root of a tree. It starts as a small grievance in the heart—“Why am I the one who always gives in?” “He has never once said thank you.” Left untended, it drives down and spreads out until one day it breaks the surface as cutting remarks, talk behind people’s backs, and factions in the group chat. It poisons not only you but many others. Discord in a family or a split in a small group often starts with one root that was never pulled up.

This week we have seen that peacemaking is the likeness of our Father; that peace isn’t pretending nothing happened; we have learned to be at peace with all as far as it depends on us and to overcome evil with good; and from Paul and Barnabas we have learned that roads that parted can meet again. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat is to ask yourself each night before bed, “Has a new root of bitterness sprung up in my heart today?” If so, hand it to God right away—don’t let it stay overnight. To multiply is to carry peace into your community: you can be the one in the group chat who defuses the fight, the one in the family who calls first, the one in the small group who says, “Let’s pray together.”

The sages of the Old Testament said it long ago: “A wrathful man stirs up contention, but one who is slow to anger appeases strife” (Proverbs 15:18). May we be the ones who calm strife—at home, in our group chats, and in the church—so that people recognize in us the likeness of God’s children.
lessons.light: Change begins with me: I don’t wait for the other person to pursue peace; I go after it first. Life first, then relationships—once the root of bitterness is pulled from the heart, relationships can bear fruit. The “9” of 920 isn’t something we recite; it is the peace the Holy Spirit plants, little by little, through each concrete “2” in our lives.
think: What warnings does Hebrews 12:14-15 connect with following after peace?
Is there a root of bitterness in my heart that I haven’t pulled up? Has it started breaking the surface?
Into which group or community will I carry peace this week? How?
lessons.speak: Father, search my heart and show me the bitterness I thought was gone but is still taking root. I hand it to You now; pull it out, root and all. And use me to be a peacemaker in my home, my group chats, and my church, so that people see the likeness of Your children. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, spend three minutes examining your heart: is there any new grievance? Write it down and give it to the Lord. Tomorrow, share one insight about reconciliation from this week with a small group companion, and pray for each other.
lessons.quick: Peace must be pursued; pull up bitterness early—don’t let it stay overnight.
text: Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees,
and make straight paths for your feet, so what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather be healed.
Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord,
looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it,

weeks.keyText: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.

weeks.title: Patience: Bearing with One Another
weeks.theme: Patience gives others time to grow, just as God has patiently kept giving me time.
group: Read Colossians 3:12-13. What identity does Paul remind us of before he tells us to bear with one another?
What kind of person do you have the least patience with? What does that reveal about your heart?
Which “slow” person are you willing to give a little more time to this week? How will you give it?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, spend time doing something alongside someone who moves at a slower pace than you: take an elderly relative for a walk, teach a family member to use their phone, sit with a child until the homework is done, or show a new friend around the market. Before you set out, pray, “Lord, lend me Your patience.” Along the way, don’t hurry them and don’t take over. Afterward, give thanks for the long patience God has shown you.

lessons.title: Put On Patience
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote to the church in Colossae, he used an everyday picture: getting dressed. First he says we “have put off the old man with his doings” (Colossians 3:9). Then he continues: “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance” (Colossians 3:12). Patience is not a personality trait you’re born with; it is a garment you deliberately put on every morning before you walk out the door.

Notice that Paul first tells us who we are: God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved. That order matters. Only someone who knows how long God has been patient with them, and how deeply they are loved, has the inner footing to be patient with others. A child who has been caught by their family again and again doesn’t panic when they fall; in the same way, a heart filled with love is not so easily provoked by other people’s weaknesses.

Then comes this week’s key verse: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13). Paul is realistic. He doesn’t assume Christians will never have complaints against each other; his “if” really means “when.” A coworker who works slowly, a roommate who never does the dishes, a friend who is always late, someone in the group chat who asks the same question over and over—these aren’t grave sins, but they wear us down the most. To “bear with” carries the sense of shouldering a load: not pretending you don’t see, but after seeing, still being willing to carry the other person and walk on together.

Why should we live this way? Because this is exactly how God treats us. “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us” (2 Peter 3:9). God gives the world time, and He gives you and me time. Patience means sharing some of the time God has given me with someone else.
lessons.light: The self-centered person lives only by their own rhythm; if others are slow, they are wrong. The selfless person knows that they, too, are growing slowly inside God’s patience. Jesus is my example: He explained things to His disciples again and again and waited for them again and again. Patience isn’t bottling up anger; it is letting the peace of Christ rule in my heart so that I can wait for others with a settled spirit.
think: In Colossians 3:12-13, who does Paul first say we are, and then what does he tell us to put on?
Who do I most easily lose patience with? Is it because they are truly wrong, or because they don’t match my rhythm?
In what situation today can I deliberately “put on” patience?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You for being so patient with me, waiting time and again for me to turn back. Today I choose to put on the patience You give as I face the people who make me anxious and hurried. Let Your peace rule in my heart, so that I don’t just hold back an outburst but truly want to carry them and walk on together. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Before you head out today, think of the person who most easily makes you impatient. When you interact with them, deliberately slow your speech and wait three extra seconds before responding. Afterward, pray one sentence for them.
lessons.quick: Patience is a garment we deliberately put on before leaving the house each day.
text: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

lessons.title: God Gives Me Time Too
lessons.hear:
A brother who leads a small group had recently been worn out by a newcomer. This new friend was late to every meeting, complained whenever it was his turn to share, never read the passage he’d agreed to read, and often sent long late-night messages pouring out his troubles. The brother thought, “I’ve already given him three chances. He doesn’t want to change. Why waste my time?”

This is an old mindset we know well: patience comes with a quota, and once it’s used up, it’s gone; if the other person doesn’t improve, they aren’t worth it. But when Paul looked back over his own life, he said something astonishing: “However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16).

Paul says he himself is a showcase of God’s patience. He “used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent” (1 Timothy 1:13), yet God did not give up on him after his third mistake. If the Lord’s patience with us ran out after three tries, which of us could still be standing? God’s view is this: a person’s growth is like a seed sprouting—it has its own timing. My job is to water, not to tug on the shoots to make them grow faster.

In prayer, that brother remembered what he had been like as a new believer: he had also shown up late and complained, and an older sister had waited for him year after year. He didn’t give up on the newcomer, but he did learn some wisdom. He gently agreed with him that late-night messages would be answered the next day, and he asked another brother in the group to walk alongside the newcomer with him, so he wasn’t carrying it alone. Six months later, the newcomer prayed aloud for someone else in small group for the first time. Patience didn’t make the problems vanish overnight, but it gave God time to work.
lessons.light: A patience with a quota is the self-centered life’s math: I expect to see a return on everything I put in. Selfless patience remembers that I, too, was the “chief of sinners” who received mercy. Patience doesn’t mean having no boundaries; it means continuing to keep a place for the other person within appropriate boundaries, quietly waiting for God’s timing.
think: In 1 Timothy 1:12-16, how does Paul describe what he used to be?
Who has been patient with me for a long time? Have I forgotten those days?
With the person who wears me out, what boundaries can I set while still walking alongside them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You displayed all Your patience in me, a sinner. Yet I often put a limit on people and shut the door when it’s used up. Remind me that I, too, have been waited for and borne with. Give me wisdom to set fitting boundaries, and give me love to keep a place for the one who wears me out. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you’re close to “giving up” on, and recall who once showed you long patience. Send that person a word of thanks, then pray for the one you feel like giving up on.
lessons.quick: If the Lord’s patience with me stopped at three, I would have fallen long ago.
text: I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service,
although I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.

lessons.title: Patient Toward All
lessons.hear:
Paul gave the church in Thessalonica a very practical “relational prescription”: “Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). It reads like a good doctor’s diagnosis: different people need different medicine, but whatever the prescription, one ingredient goes into every dose—patience.

This shows us that patience isn’t a one-note “just keep your mouth shut.” With the disorderly, patience is a gentle but clear reminder rather than a sudden explosion. With the faint-hearted, patience is encouraging them again and again without minding that they keep describing the same struggle. With the weak, patience is slowing down to walk beside them and hold them up without resenting that they slow you down. The wise man says, “The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11). Discretion means being able to tell which medicine the person in front of you needs.

Today, choose one person and put this into practice. Maybe it’s a new coworker who always turns in work late—you could spend ten minutes showing them a method instead of complaining behind their back. Maybe it’s an older relative who keeps forwarding fake news in the family group chat—you could explain gently in private instead of correcting them publicly and making them lose face. Maybe it’s a friend who keeps sinking into the same low place—you could listen to them one more time and help them think of one small next step. If their low mood doesn’t lift over a long period, you can also gently encourage them to seek counseling or medical help; that, too, is God’s grace.

At the same time, remember that being patient toward all doesn’t mean you must carry everyone by yourself. Paul addressed these words to the “brothers”; patience is a lesson the whole community carries together. You take your share, and you can invite others to share the load too.
lessons.light: When Paul describes love, his very first words are “Love is patient” (1 Corinthians 13:4). Patience is not passive endurance; it is active companionship. 920 reminds me that every person connected to me is one of my “2.” Some of my “2” walk quickly and some walk slowly, and the Holy Spirit wants to grow in me a life that can keep pace with different strides.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 5:14, what three kinds of people does Paul mention, and what does each need?
Which kind is the “slow” person in my life? What wrong medicine have I been giving?
Toward whom will I practice which kind of patience today?
lessons.speak: Father, You know I often treat everyone the same way, and I end up hurting people and exhausting myself. Give me discretion to see what each person around me needs: a gentle reminder for those who need reminding, encouragement again and again for those who need encouraging, and a slower pace for those who need support. And keep me from carrying it all alone; teach me to share the load with my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pick one “slow” person and be patient with them once in the way they need: show a coworker a method, gently explain something to an older relative in private, or listen to a friend one more time and help them think of a next step.
lessons.quick: Different people need different medicine, but every dose needs patience.
text: But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,
and to respect and honor them in love for their work’s sake. Be at peace among yourselves.
We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.
See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.

lessons.title: The Sons of Thunder
lessons.hear:
James and John had a nickname: “Boanerges, which means, Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). Luke records one of the reasons they earned it. When a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus, the two brothers immediately asked, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?” (Luke 9:54). They had even found a Bible story to back up their temper.

Jesus’ response was clear: “But he turned and rebuked them, ‘You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are. For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them’” (Luke 9:55-56). And then, “They went to another village.” The Lord did not answer anger with anger, nor did He stay put to prove Himself. He simply went on to another village and kept walking toward the cross.

Let this passage hold up a mirror to you. First, have I also wrapped my impatience in “spiritual reasons”? “I’m standing up for the truth,” “I’m just being honest”—when really, in my heart, it’s the anger of feeling offended. Second, do I feel that being rejected means being humiliated? The fire of the Sons of Thunder often burns not for the Lord but for their own pride. Third, do I really know what kind of spirit I am of? Often we don’t realize how quick-tempered we are until the words are out of our mouths or the message has been sent. “He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly” (Proverbs 14:29).

The good news is that Sons of Thunder can be changed. That same John, in the letters he wrote in his later years, says “love one another” again and again, and later generations called him the apostle of love. The path of adjustment is to let Jesus “turn” and speak to us again and again. When we’re willing to listen, we learn His way: we don’t burn down the village; we take another road and keep on loving.
lessons.light: The temper of the Sons of Thunder is the self-centered life: if you won’t welcome me, I’ll make you pay. The patience of Jesus is selfless: His focus is on saving people, not on saving face. Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, not the head and our own strength—when anger rises, first let the Lord turn and speak to me. Then I don’t need to rush to call down fire; I can take another road and keep on loving.
think: In Luke 9:51-56, what did Jesus do after being rejected, and what did He not do?
Have I ever found a “spiritual” reason to justify my anger?
The next time my temper flares, what sentence will I use to remind myself to stop?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, when You were rejected, You didn’t call down fire; You turned toward another village and kept walking the road of saving people. I confess I am often as quick-tempered as the Sons of Thunder, and I even find reasons for my anger. Turn and speak to me, change my heart, and make me like John—transformed from a son of thunder into a disciple of love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, recall the last time you lost your temper or said something harsh. If the other person was hurt, apologize briefly and sincerely. Then copy out Luke 9:56 and keep it next to your phone.
lessons.quick: A son of thunder can become an apostle of love—if we let Jesus turn and speak.
text: It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem
and sent messengers before his face. They went and entered into a village of the Samaritans, so as to prepare for him.
They didn’t receive him, because he was traveling with his face set toward Jerusalem.
When his disciples, James and John, saw this, they said, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?”
But he turned and rebuked them, “You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are.
For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them.” They went to another village.

lessons.title: The Patience of a Farmer
lessons.hear:
James uses a farmer to illustrate patience: “Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain” (James 5:7). A farmer doesn’t dig up the seeds every day to see whether they’ve grown, and he doesn’t shout at the seedlings to hurry up. He does what he’s supposed to do—sow, weed, water—and then he waits. His patience isn’t passive staring into space; it is hope-filled waiting, because he knows the harvest will surely come.

Relationships are a field too. You’ve smiled at a distant neighbor for a year, and they still barely respond. You’ve shared the gospel with a friend many times, and they still aren’t interested. You’ve walked with a family member through a dark valley, and progress seems painfully slow. James reminds us: don’t dig up the seeds to check. God has His early and late rain.

James goes on: “Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged” (James 5:9). While we wait, grumbling is what springs up most easily: grumbling that the other person isn’t growing, and grumbling that other brothers and sisters aren’t helping. Grumbling is like hail; one storm can ruin a whole season’s crop.

This week we learned to put on patience, to remember that God gives me time too, to see that different people need different medicine, and, from the Sons of Thunder, that the Lord can change a quick temper. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat is to ask once a day, “Whom did I give time to today?” To multiply is to tell someone the story of how you have been shown patience, so they too can know that “the Lord is full of compassion and mercy” (James 5:11). A person who has been shown patience and has learned to be patient with others is a living gospel.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry: patience is not a technique but the fruit of a life. The farmer trusts the early and late rain; we trust the Holy Spirit. To let Jesus reign is to admit that the time of harvest is in His hands. My part is to sow and water faithfully every day, without grumbling and without giving up.
think: Whom does James 5:7-11 hold up as examples of patience?
In which relationship have I kept wanting to dig up the seeds to check?
Whom will I tell my story of being shown patience?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You that You are full of compassion and mercy. Teach me to be like a farmer in my relationships—sowing faithfully and waiting patiently, without grumbling and without giving up. And use the story of Your patience with me to encourage someone else who is waiting right now. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find a small group companion or a friend and take five minutes to share how God or someone else showed you long patience. Then ask them, “Which relationship are you waiting to see change right now?” and pray for them.
lessons.quick: Don’t dig up the seeds to check; God has His early and late rain.
text: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Behold, the judge stands at the door.
Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of perseverance, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

weeks.keyText: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

weeks.title: Kindness: A Tender Heart
weeks.theme: Kindness is goodwill that takes the initiative: reaching out first, even when the other person doesn’t deserve it.
group: Read Ephesians 4:31-32. What does Paul tell us to put away first, and what are we to take up instead?
Do you keep a mental “ledger of favors” in your heart? How does it affect the way you treat people?
Toward which “undeserving” person are you willing to reach out first this week, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, prepare a “seat at the table” for someone who is often overlooked: invite a less-connected member of your small group, an elderly person who lives alone, or a newly arrived immigrant to share a meal, or bring a homemade treat when you go to visit them. Before you set out, pray that the Lord would help you see people the way He sees them. Afterward, thank God for the kindness He showed you first.

lessons.title: Be Kind to One Another
lessons.hear:
Some virtues are about holding back—not lying, not stealing. Kindness is about giving. Paul says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). Kindness isn’t merely not hurting people; it’s actively doing them good. It doesn’t wait for others to ask; it notices their needs first.

Look at Paul’s order. Right before this verse he says, “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). It’s like tidying a house: first you haul out the piled-up trash, and then guests have somewhere to sit. A heart stuffed with bitterness finds it very hard to be kind—not because it doesn’t want to, but because there’s no room. So the first step of kindness is often to be emptied out before God.

Kindness shows up first in our words. Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). “As the need may be” means paying attention to timing and need: to someone who is tired, “Thank you for all your hard work”; to someone who has made a mistake, “Let’s figure this out together”; to someone who has been left out, “I’m really glad you came.” A single kind word often stays in someone’s heart longer than an expensive gift.

The source of kindness is in the last phrase: “just as God also in Christ forgave you.” We didn’t become good people first so that God would be kind to us; God was kind first to us, who didn’t deserve it. People who have received kindness pass it on, like a river that has been filled flowing naturally downstream. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to clear out room in your heart so God’s kindness can flow through you to someone else.
lessons.light: Self-centered goodwill is a transaction: I’ll be good to you if you’re good to me. Selfless kindness is like God’s: it gives first, gives freely, and gives to the undeserving. When the mindset changes, the life changes—once I truly understand that I have been shown kindness freely, I can close my “ledger of favors” and open a “ledger of grace” instead.
think: In Ephesians 4:29-32, what does Paul tell us to put away, and how are we to treat one another?
Lately, have my words built people up more often, or hurt them more often?
To whom can I speak a word today that builds them up “as the need may be”?
lessons.speak: Father, You forgave me in Christ; You were kind first to me, though I didn’t deserve it. Clear away the bitterness and resentment in my heart and make room for Your kindness. Today, guard my mouth so that I speak what builds others up as the need may be, giving grace to those who hear. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, say one specific, encouraging word—in person or by message—to someone who is tired, has made a mistake, or has been left out. For example: “Thank you for doing ___. I noticed.”
lessons.quick: Kindness isn’t merely not hurting people; it’s actively doing them good.
text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: For Jonathan’s Sake
lessons.hear:
A brother who had been doing well at his company was recently promoted to team lead. The coworker who had competed with him for the position was transferred to an out-of-the-way department and often sat alone in a corner at lunch. People on the team said, “He talked about you behind your back so much—now he gets a taste of his own medicine.” Deep down, the brother felt a bit satisfied too.

This is an old mindset we know well: kindness should go to people who deserve it; favors should be returned in kind; and if someone has treated me badly, at least I don’t have to bother with them. But David’s story shows us God’s point of view.
