After David became king, the first thing he took the initiative to ask was, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” (2 Samuel 9:3). Saul had hunted David for years, and by the custom of the time, a new king would wipe out the previous dynasty’s descendants. David instead went looking for someone to show favor to.

The one they found was Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, lame in both feet. As soon as he saw David he bowed down and said, “What is your servant, that you should look at such a dead dog as I am?” (2 Samuel 9:8). David didn’t just give back the family land; he said, “You will eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7). Kindness isn’t only giving things; it’s giving someone a place—seating a person who thinks they don’t deserve it at the king’s table.

Later, in prayer, that brother remembered that he, too, had once been like “a dead dog,” yet the Lord had invited him to His banquet. The next day he carried his lunch box over to that coworker’s table: “Mind if I join you?” The coworker was startled, and the meal was a little awkward. But a few weeks later, when the coworker got stuck on a work problem, the first person he came to was this brother. Kindness didn’t erase the past, but it opened up a new future.
lessons.light: David showed favor not because Mephibosheth deserved it, but “for Jonathan … sake”; God is kind to us for Christ’s sake. Selfless kindness doesn’t ask whether the other person deserves it; it only asks, “How much have I received in Christ?” To let Jesus reign is to let the rules of His table replace my ledger of favors.
think: In 2 Samuel 9, what are the things David did for Mephibosheth?
Is there someone I secretly feel is just “getting what they deserve”?
How can I make room for someone who has been left out to have a “seat at the table”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I was once like Mephibosheth, feeling unworthy, yet You invited me to sit at Your banquet. Forgive me for measuring others by my ledger of favors, and even quietly hoping some people would suffer a little. Give me David’s heart to go looking for the one who has been left out and to give them a place. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, take the initiative to invite someone who has been left out, or someone you’ve had friction with, to lunch or a drink—or make a point of welcoming them by name at a group activity.
lessons.quick: Kindness isn’t only giving things; it’s giving someone a place.
text: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”
He bowed down, and said, “What is your servant, that you should look at such a dead dog as I am?”
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s son.

Till the land for him—you, your sons, and your servants. Bring in the harvest, that your master’s son may have bread to eat; but Mephibosheth your master’s son will always eat bread at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Then Ziba said to the king, “According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so your servant will do.” So Mephibosheth ate at the king’s table like one of the king’s sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. All who lived in Ziba’s house were servants to Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate continually at the king’s table. He was lame in both his feet.

lessons.title: Do Good to Those Who Hate You
lessons.hear:
Jesus’ words often go further than we expect: “love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you” (Luke 6:27-28). Four actions, each one going a step further than the last: from love in the heart, to good done with the hands, to blessing spoken with the mouth, to prayer offered on our knees.

Why live this way? Jesus gives the reason a few verses later: then “you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil” (Luke 6:35). The sun shines on the good and the bad alike; God’s kindness never checks someone’s qualifications first. When we are kind to the undeserving, we are living out our Father’s likeness.

Start with something small today. Think: who has made you uncomfortable lately? Maybe a neighbor who keeps parking badly downstairs, a coworker who took credit for your work in a meeting, or a relative who leaves snide comments on your posts. Choose one of them today and do one thing that “does good” to them: pick up a package left at your neighbor’s door, mention your coworker’s contribution in front of your manager, or leave a sincere blessing under your relative’s post. And pray a specific prayer for that person—not asking God to set them straight, but asking God to bless them.

One word of caution: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30) doesn’t mean throwing away wisdom. Kindness isn’t the same as enabling, nor does it mean lending money you can’t afford to lose. If fraud, extortion, or ongoing harm is involved, protecting yourself and your family and seeking help from someone you trust or a professional is also love. The overall principle Jesus gives us is this: “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them” (Luke 6:31). First think about how you’d like to be treated, then go and treat others that way first.
lessons.light: Repaying evil with evil is the instinct of the self-centered life; answering evil with kindness is the life of Christ in me. Love gives first; it doesn’t trade. The “2” of 920 includes the people who make me uncomfortable, and in my dealings with them the Holy Spirit wants to bear the fruit of kindness that I could never produce on my own. When I use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, I can go the extra mile.
think: In Luke 6:27-28, what four things does Jesus tell us to do toward our enemies?
Who has made me uncomfortable lately? Do I want to bless them, or see them lose out?
What specific good thing will I do for that person today, and what blessing will I speak?
lessons.speak: Father, You are kind toward the unthankful and evil, and You were kind to me when I was rebellious. Today I bring before You the person who makes me uncomfortable; please bless them. Give me strength to do one good thing for them, and give me wisdom to discern boundaries, so that my kindness is, like Yours, both genuine and clear-eyed. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone who makes you uncomfortable and do one specific good thing for them (pick up a package, mention their contribution, leave a blessing), and pray specifically for them once.
lessons.quick: Think how you’d like to be treated—then go and treat others that way first.
text: “But I tell you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.
To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other; and from him who takes away your cloak, don’t withhold your coat also.
Give to everyone who asks you, and don’t ask him who takes away your goods to give them back again.
“As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.

lessons.title: Put Down the Stone
lessons.hear:
Early that morning, the temple courts were packed with people listening to Jesus teach. The scribes and Pharisees brought in a woman, and “having set her in the middle” (John 8:3), they spoke as though they only cared about keeping the law of Moses. But their real aim is spelled out plainly: “They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of” (John 8:6). In their eyes, this woman wasn’t a person but a tool. Stranger still, why was she the only one caught in the act? The law held both parties equally guilty (see Leviticus 20:10), yet they brought only the one who was easier to push around.

This is a very uncomfortable mirror. We often hold stones in our hands too: a screenshot we forward, a bit of gossip that begins, “I heard that he …” We have a thousand excuses for our own weaknesses and only one verdict for other people’s faults. Grace for myself, law for everyone else—that is the double standard of the self-centered life.

Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground, then straightened up and said, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her” (John 8:7). Scripture says they “went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last” (John 8:9). Perhaps the older they were, the better they remembered how much grace they owed. Jesus didn’t say sin doesn’t matter; He turned the light away from the woman and shone it into the heart of every person holding a stone.

In the end, only one person remained who had any right to throw a stone, and He said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). That is kindness: not pretending nothing happened, but first giving a person a way to live, and then calling them to walk a new way.

Today, review honestly: whose stone am I holding? Do I see a person, or just a juicy topic? The path of adjustment is simple and hard: put the stone down, starting with that one forwarded message. Those who turned and walked away at least put down their stones; the Lord is waiting for us to do the same.
lessons.light: Those holding stones are sitting in the judge’s seat—leaving our proper place and trying to take God’s. Humility is returning to our proper place: I, too, am a sinner who has received mercy. Selfless kindness doesn’t deny sin, but like Jesus, it first gives people a way to live. When I shift from the human point of view to God’s, I stop collecting other people’s offenses and remember the forgiveness I have received.
think: In John 8:3-11, how does Jesus deal with both the accusers and the woman?
Whose “stone” am I holding right now—a screenshot, or a piece of gossip?
How will I put down that stone today and give that person a way to live?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often hold stones in my hands—lenient with myself, harsh with others. Thank You that You did not condemn me, but gave me a way to live. Help me put down my judgments and, like You, lead with a tender heart. And help both me and others walk in a new way from now on. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, delete a screenshot or message you were planning to forward that discusses someone’s faults. Then pray for that person, asking the Lord to give them a way forward.
lessons.quick: The only One who could throw a stone chose not to condemn.
text: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them.
The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle,
they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act.
Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?”
They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.”
Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.
Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?”
She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”

lessons.title: When Kindness Appeared
lessons.hear:
In his letter to Titus, Paul describes very honestly what we used to be like: “For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (Titus 3:3). He isn’t talking about other people; he’s talking about “we.” If you posted that as your social media bio, it probably wouldn’t get many likes.

Then comes the turn: when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us” (Titus 3:5). Kindness isn’t a reward we earn by effort; it is God breaking in on us at our least lovable moments. Elsewhere Paul reminds us that “the goodness of God leads you to repentance” (see Romans 2:4). People aren’t changed by being scolded; they are melted by kindness.

This week we have seen that kindness is goodwill that takes the initiative; learned from David that kindness gives people a place; practiced doing good to those who hate us; and, in those holding stones, seen our own double standards. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat is to remind yourself every day, “I was also once …”—then it’s much harder to look down on anyone. To multiply is to pass kindness on: teach your children to greet the classmate who is always alone, invite your small group to prepare a meal together for a family in need, or tell the story of the kindness you received to a friend who is struggling.

Kindness is like a lamp: when it lights the next one, it loses none of its own light, and the whole room grows brighter. Today, who will see, because of you, that God’s kindness has appeared?
lessons.light: “I was also once …” is the key to humility: remembering the kindness I received makes me kind to others. This is the heart of 920: I am a “2” transformed by God’s “9,” and now I carry that fruit to the next “2.” The final step of the eight steps of changing a mindset is multiplication: passing on the flame of grace.
think: In Titus 3:3-5, how does Paul describe what we used to be and what God has done?
Have I forgotten that I “was also once” unlovable?
To whom will I pass on kindness this week, or whom will I invite to do an act of kindness with me?
lessons.speak: Father, I was once foolish, disobedient, and hateful, yet You saved me according to Your mercy. Never let me forget this kindness. Make me a lamp that passes it on, and help me bring my family and my small group along to show kindness to those in need. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a family member or small group companion to do an act of kindness together for someone in need (bring a meal, write a card, go with them to a doctor’s appointment), and pray for that person together first.
lessons.quick: People aren’t changed by being scolded; they are melted by kindness.
text: For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior;
that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

weeks.keyText: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

weeks.title: Goodness: Not Weary in Doing Good
weeks.theme: Goodness is good seed sown again and again; those who don’t give up will reap in due season.
group: Read Galatians 6:7-10. What is Paul illustrating with sowing and reaping?
In which relationship have you done good until you grew weary? What was going through your mind then?
To which neighbor are you willing to keep doing one good thing this week, and how will you do it?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, do one good deed that is “bread cast on the waters”: pitch in to clean up your neighborhood, fix something small for an elderly person who lives alone, or prepare a snack and a thank-you card for your building’s security guard or cleaner. Before you go, pray and entrust this act of goodness to God. Afterward, expect nothing in return—simply thank God for the opportunity to do good.

lessons.title: Let’s Not Be Weary
lessons.hear:
At the end of Galatians, Paul uses a principle every farmer understands: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Plant watermelons and you get watermelons; plant thorns and you get thorns. Relationships are a field too: the words we say, the things we do, and the messages we send each day are all seeds. Sow indifference and you reap distance; sow judgment and you reap defensiveness; sow goodness and you reap trust.

Then comes this week’s key verse: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9). Why does Paul specifically warn us not to be weary? Because the greatest enemy of doing good isn’t evil people; it’s discouragement. You’ve looked after a sick neighbor several times, and they’ve never once said thank you. You quietly organize information for the group chat, and all anyone does is point out mistakes. You keep being gentle with your family, and they take it for granted. At that point a voice inside says, “Forget it. Nice guys finish last.”

But Paul says “in due season.” Once a seed is buried in the soil, there is a stretch of time when it is completely invisible. That isn’t failure; that’s growth. God remembers every seed you have sown, and He will make it sprout in His time—sometimes in this life, sometimes in eternity.

So Paul sums it up: “So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith” (Galatians 6:10). Goodness isn’t a one-time act of heroism; it’s an ongoing way of life. It doesn’t wait for a “big opportunity”; it seizes the small ones that come every day. Today you will meet several such opportunities. Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to see them.
lessons.light: Goodness isn’t having a nice personality; it is sowing in step with the Holy Spirit. Self-centered good deeds keep count of the return, and when the return doesn’t come, they grow weary. Selfless good deeds hand the harvest over to God, and so they can keep going. From a temporary to an eternal point of view: not one piece of fruit we can’t see today will be missing from God’s ledger, and in due season we will reap.
think: In Galatians 6:7-10, what two kinds of sowing does Paul describe, and what does each reap?
In which act of goodness am I close to growing weary?
What “small opportunity” to do good can I seize today?
lessons.speak: Father, You see the good deeds no one notices and no one thanks me for, and You know that sometimes I’ve already lost heart. Renew my strength so that I look not at people’s responses but at Your promise. Today, open my eyes to every small opportunity to do good, and help me sow in step with the Holy Spirit. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify one good thing you stopped doing because you got discouraged (checking in on someone, helping with something) and do it again. At the same time, pray for the person who has never responded.
lessons.quick: The greatest enemy of doing good isn’t evil people; it’s discouragement.
text: But let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches.
Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.title: The Garments Dorcas Made
lessons.hear:
A sister who had just retired often felt she was “not much use” at church. She couldn’t preach, couldn’t lead worship, and didn’t know her way around a computer. All she could do was cook a pot of soup for brothers and sisters who were sick, or sit beside a newcomer at their first meeting and help them find the Bible passage. She would often say, “Everything I do is small stuff. I can’t compare with people who have real gifts.”

This is a common old mindset: goodness only counts if it’s big and gets noticed. But Luke records a disciple who did almost nothing but “small stuff”: “Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did” (Acts 9:36). After Dorcas died, the widows gathered around Peter weeping, “showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them” (Acts 9:39).

Picture the scene. Nobody brought out her sermons or her project proposals. What they brought out were garments, one after another. Each was cut to fit a particular widow; every stitch was sewn with care. Those garments were her résumé. In God’s kingdom, what is remembered isn’t our titles but the people we have loved.

Then God raised Dorcas to life through Peter, and “this became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord” (Acts 9:42). A sister who quietly sewed clothes became the doorway through which a whole city came to know the Lord. When the retired sister read this passage in her small group, she wept. She finally understood that her soup and her companionship were not small things; they were the needle and thread of God’s kingdom. Later, a young man she had helped find Bible passages said the reason he stayed was this: “There was an auntie who always sat next to me.”
lessons.light: Self-centered goodness wants to be seen, so it only does big things. Selfless goodness gladly does small things, because its focus is on people, not on applause. Let Jesus receive all the glory: Dorcas left behind no famous sayings, only garments, and through those garments God drew many to Himself. Small things done for people are big things.
think: In Acts 9:36-42, what did the widows bring out to remember Dorcas?
Have I been underestimating the “small things” I am doing right now?
For whom around me can I sew a “garment” made just for them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for remembering every small thing done out of love. Forgive me for wanting to do big things and be noticed, while overlooking the real needs around me. Make me like Dorcas, using what is already in my hands to love the people near me faithfully, and receive glory through these small things. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, use what you already have to do a “Dorcas-style” good deed for a specific person: make some soup, mend a garment, or go with them to take care of an errand—no need to tell anyone.
lessons.quick: In God’s kingdom, what is remembered isn’t our titles but the people we have loved.
text: Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.
In those days, she became sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them.

Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.

lessons.title: Don’t Say “Come Back Tomorrow”
lessons.hear:
Solomon gives us a very direct reminder: “Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it” (Proverbs 3:27). He follows right away with: “Don’t say to your neighbor, ‘Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,’ when you have it by you” (Proverbs 3:28).

“Come back tomorrow” is a trap for many well-meaning people. It’s not that we don’t want to do good; it’s “when I have more time,” “when I have more money,” “once this busy stretch is over.” So we promise to look over a friend’s résumé and let it slide for three weeks. We say we’ll visit a hospitalized coworker and wait until they’ve been discharged. Someone in the group chat asks who can help them move, and after thinking it over, we wait for someone else to answer first. And so the seeds of goodness sit in our pockets day after day, going moldy.

Today, put this into practice with three questions. First, what do I “have by me”? It doesn’t have to be money—it might be a skill, a little time, a connection, or a word of encouragement. Second, who are the people “to whom it is due”? They are the ones God has placed near you whose needs you can clearly see. Third, what good thing have I already promised but kept putting off? Get it done today.

Solomon goes on: “Don’t devise evil against your neighbor, since he dwells securely by you” (Proverbs 3:29). Doing good also includes not doing things that quietly hurt others: not spreading gossip about them, and not undermining their interests at the homeowners’ association meeting for your own convenience. Of course, doing good also takes wisdom. When it involves large sums of money, meeting someone you only know online, or being alone with someone of the opposite sex, be careful, and when necessary bring along a trusted brother or sister. Goodness isn’t naïveté; it is loving with clear eyes and good timing.
lessons.light: Of the eight steps of changing a mindset, practice is the one most easily stuck at “tomorrow.” A life of goodness is lived out today. People matter more than things: rather than waiting for the perfect moment to do something grand, do one small, ready-to-hand good thing today for a “2” right next to you. One step today beats ten steps tomorrow.
think: In Proverbs 3:27-30, what does Solomon list as things to do and things not to do?
What good thing have I promised but kept putting off?
What do I “have by me” that I can give away today?
lessons.speak: Father, I often tell people “come back tomorrow,” leaving the goodness You entrusted to me to go moldy in my pocket. Forgive my procrastination. Today, open my eyes to the grace already in my hands and to the people near me to whom it is due, and give me wisdom and courage to do good promptly and with clear eyes. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, finish one good thing you promised but have kept putting off (a reply, a favor, a visit, or a recommendation), and when it’s done, pray one sentence for that person.
lessons.quick: Seeds of goodness left in your pocket too long go moldy.
text: Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it.
Don’t say to your neighbor, “Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you have it by you.
Don’t devise evil against your neighbor, since he dwells securely by you.
Don’t strive with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm.

lessons.title: One Thing You Lack
lessons.hear:
A man came running, knelt before Jesus, and asked with great sincerity, “Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” (Mark 10:17). He was wealthy, well-bred, and eager. But Jesus first replied, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God” (Mark 10:18). From the very first words, Jesus brought goodness back to God.

Then Jesus listed commandments, all of them about our neighbors: do not murder, do not steal, do not give false testimony, do not defraud, honor your father and mother. The man answered, “Teacher, I have observed all these things from my youth” (Mark 10:20). Much of our goodness is like that: I don’t gossip, I don’t owe anyone money, I’m polite to people, so I’m a good person. But there is still a long road between “not doing bad things” and “doing good things for people.”

Then comes the tenderest line in the whole passage: “Jesus looking at him loved him” (Mark 10:21). Before saying the hardest thing, the Lord first looked at him with eyes of love. Only then did He say, “One thing you lack.” The man had great possessions, and those possessions had quietly taken the throne of his heart. His goodness could go a long way, but it stopped short when it ran into the thing he treasured most. And so “his face fell at that saying, and he went away sorrowful” (Mark 10:22).

Today, let this passage help you review: where does my goodness stop? Maybe at my weekend rest, the money in my bank account, or the pride that refuses to be looked down on. The Lord doesn’t necessarily ask everyone to sell everything, but He will point to that “one thing” in your heart and gently ask: will you let go of it for Me and for your neighbor?

The good news is that the story doesn’t end with a sigh. Jesus said to His dismayed disciples, “With men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God” (Mark 10:27). Goodness we squeeze out on our own stops short at the price; goodness that comes from God can make us open our hands. Adjustment begins today with letting go of one thing.
lessons.light: Self-centered goodness is a checklist: I haven’t done anything bad, so I’m a good person. Selfless goodness is a question of the throne: who reigns in my heart? When possessions, time, or pride reign, goodness turns and walks away when faced with the cost. Let Jesus reign, and He will turn the one thing I lack into the one thing I give away.
think: In Mark 10:17-22, what did Jesus do before speaking the hard word?
Where does my goodness usually stop—at time, money, or pride?
What “one thing” am I willing to let go of for my neighbor today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often think I’m a good person because I haven’t done anything bad, yet I turn away when it’s time to pay the price. Thank You for looking at me and still loving me. Show me the one thing my heart is clutching, and give me courage to let go of it for You and for my neighbor. Where I cannot, show Your power. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify the one thing you’re clutching—perhaps time, money, or your quiet—and give part of it to a specific neighbor, for example by setting aside an hour to keep them company.
lessons.quick: Not doing harm isn’t enough; goodness has to get past the one thing I’m clutching.
text: As he was going out into the way, one ran to him, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?”
Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.
You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder,’ ‘Do not commit adultery,’ ‘Do not steal,’ ‘Do not give false testimony,’ ‘Do not defraud,’ ‘Honor your father and mother.’”
He said to him, “Teacher, I have observed all these things from my youth.”
Jesus looking at him loved him, and said to him, “One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross.”
But his face fell at that saying, and he went away sorrowful, for he was one who had great possessions.

lessons.title: Sow in the Morning, Don’t Rest in the Evening
lessons.hear:
The Teacher gives us a curious picture: “Cast your bread on the waters; for you shall find it after many days” (Ecclesiastes 11:1). Throwing bread on the water looks like a waste—it drifts away and disappears from sight. But the Teacher says you will find it after many days. Much goodness is like that: you don’t know where that word of encouragement drifted, or when that one act of help will blossom—but God knows.

He continues: “He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap” (Ecclesiastes 11:4). We often wait for conditions to be right before we do good: until I’m less busy, until the other person is easier to get along with, until I’m sure it will work. But people who are forever watching the wind and the clouds never get a single seed into the ground. The Teacher’s conclusion is simple: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper” (Ecclesiastes 11:6).

This week we have seen that we must not grow weary in doing good; seen in Dorcas the weight of small things; learned not to tell our neighbor “come back tomorrow”; and seen, in the man who went away sorrowful, that true goodness comes from God. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat is to make doing good a daily rhythm, as natural as brushing your teeth in the morning: do at least one small good thing for one person every day. To multiply is to bring others along to sow with you: invite a small group companion, a family member, or your kids to “adopt” a neighbor who needs care, and take turns visiting them and praying for them.

Paul says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). Doing good isn’t an extra ministry; it is what we were created for. So today, go and sow your seed.
lessons.light: When doing good becomes a rhythm, goodness becomes a life. 235 reminds me that sowing alongside spiritual companions goes further than sowing alone. To let Jesus reign is to hand the harvest to Him: I sow, He grows. I don’t watch the wind or study the clouds; I fix my eyes on Him and keep sowing.
think: What images does the Teacher use for sowing in Ecclesiastes 11:1-6?
Do I often “watch the wind and the clouds,” waiting for conditions to be right before doing good?
Whom will I invite this week to join me in adopting a neighbor who needs care?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You for creating me in Christ for good works. Rescue me from the hesitation that only watches the wind and the clouds, and help me sow in the morning and not withhold my hand in the evening. Give me companions to sow goodness together in our neighborhood, our workplaces, and online, so that Your name is glorified. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a family member or small group companion to adopt a neighbor or elderly person who needs care together. Set a time to visit, bring a meal, or call to check in.
lessons.quick: Whoever watches the wind won’t sow; get your seed into the ground today.
text: Cast your bread on the waters; for you shall find it after many days.
Give a portion to seven, yes, even to eight; for you don’t know what evil will be on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth; and if a tree falls toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there shall it be.
He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.
As you don’t know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child; even so you don’t know the work of God who does all.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.

weeks.keyText: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.

weeks.title: Faithfulness: A Friend You Can Trust
weeks.theme: Faithfulness means keeping your word, keeping confidences, and never walking away in hard times.
group: Read 1 Samuel 20:12-17. What marks of faithfulness do you see in Jonathan’s friendship?
Have you ever been let down or abandoned by a friend? How has that affected the way you make friends?
For which friend going through hard times are you willing to “show up” this week, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, call or meet up with an old friend you were once close to but haven’t been in touch with for a long time, or visit a friend who is going through a low season. Before you go, pray that the Lord would make you someone people can trust. When you meet, listen more than you talk, and keep what they share with you in confidence. Afterward, thank God for His unchanging faithfulness.

lessons.title: A Friend Loves at All Times
lessons.hear:
Solomon describes a true friend in a single line: “A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity” (Proverbs 17:17). The words “at all times” matter. Loving someone when things are going well isn’t hard. What’s hard is still loving them when they’ve lost standing, when trouble hits, when people are talking about them. Adversity is like an X-ray: it shows who is a fair-weather friend and who is a friend for life.

The most moving friendship in the Bible is between Jonathan and David. Jonathan was the prince, the one with the best claim to the throne; David, though, had been anointed by God and had become a thorn in the side of Jonathan’s father, Saul. By human reckoning, Jonathan should have sided with his father and gotten rid of his rival. Instead, he chose faithfulness. At the risk of enraging his father, he gathered information for David and swore that if his father meant David harm and he didn’t warn him, the Lord should deal with him severely (see 1 Samuel 20:13). Scripture says, “Jonathan caused David to swear again, for the love that he had for him; for he loved him as he loved his own soul” (1 Samuel 20:17).

Jonathan’s faithfulness had three marks. First, he kept his word: having promised to warn David, he took the risk and did it. Second, he set aside his own interests: for his friend’s sake, he was willing to give up the throne. Third, his commitment reached to the next generation: he asked David, “you shall also not cut off your kindness from my house forever” (1 Samuel 20:15), and years later David did indeed show kindness to his son Mephibosheth.

Where does faithfulness like this come from? From God. Jonathan swore again and again “by the Lord,” because he knew that human loyalty can falter, but God is faithful. We can become trustworthy friends not because we are reliable by nature, but because the God who never breaks His word lives in us. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: who needs you to be their Jonathan?
lessons.light: Faithfulness is a fruit of the Spirit—the steadiness of Christ’s life in our relationships. Self-centered friendship asks whether the other person benefits me; selfless friendship, like Jonathan’s, is glad to see a friend do better than I do. The “2” of 920 isn’t a one-time acquaintance but someone God has entrusted to me to keep faith with over the long haul and to love for a lifetime.
think: In 1 Samuel 20:12-17, what did Jonathan promise David?
Does my friendship love “at all times,” or only when things are going well?
Who is going through adversity and needs me to be their Jonathan?
lessons.speak: Father, You are the God who never breaks His word. Thank You for never leaving me in my troubles. Make me a faithful friend too—loving in good times and even more in hard times, keeping my word, and glad to see my friends do better than I do. Today, show me who needs me to stand beside them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a friend who is going through a hard time (job loss, illness, family upheaval, being talked about), and send them a message: “I’ve been thinking of you and praying for you. Reach out anytime you need me.”
lessons.quick: Adversity is a mirror that shows who your true friends are.
text: Jonathan said to David, “By the LORD, the God of Israel, when I have sounded out my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if there is good toward David, won’t I then send to you and disclose it to you?

The LORD do so to Jonathan and more also, should it please my father to do you evil, if I don’t disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in peace. May the LORD be with you as he has been with my father.
You shall not only show me the loving kindness of the LORD while I still live, that I not die;
but you shall also not cut off your kindness from my house forever, no, not when the LORD has cut off every one of the enemies of David from the surface of the earth.”
So Jonathan made a covenant with David’s house, saying, “The LORD will require it at the hand of David’s enemies.”
Jonathan caused David to swear again, for the love that he had for him; for he loved him as he loved his own soul.

lessons.title: Keeping an Oath Even When It Hurts
lessons.hear:
A young man fresh out of college had promised to help a close friend from university move on Saturday. On Thursday night, his manager suddenly invited him to an important client dinner that Saturday—a rare chance to make a good impression. He weighed it in his mind: “My friend can find someone else to help him move. He’ll understand.” He very nearly typed “Sorry, something came up” in the group chat.

This is an old mindset we know well: commitments depend on circumstances; if a better opportunity comes along, you can change your plans; small promises don’t matter, and friends should understand anyway. But Psalm 15 asks a big question: “LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?” (Psalm 15:1). Part of the answer cuts deep: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” (Psalm 15:4).

Faithful people don’t keep their word only when it’s convenient; they keep it even when it costs them. Their “yes” means “yes,” and their word carries weight. The psalmist also describes such a person as one “who doesn’t slander with his tongue, nor does evil to his friend, nor casts slurs against his fellow man” (Psalm 15:3). Faithfulness isn’t only showing up on time; it also means keeping your friends’ secrets, not joining in the gossip in the group chat, and not undercutting a friend behind their back.

In the end, the brother politely replied to his manager that he had already promised a friend for Saturday and asked whether they could meet another time. His manager was a little surprised, but didn’t think less of him—in fact, from then on he often gave him work that required trustworthiness. More importantly, after the move was done, his friend said to him, standing among the stacks of boxes, “I knew you’d come.” That one sentence was worth more than any dinner.
lessons.light: Not keeping my word puts me above others: my convenience matters more than your need. Selfless faithfulness is willing to take a loss to keep a promise, because for someone who lets Jesus reign, even a small promise is made before God. People matter more than things, and trustworthiness is worth more than opportunity. Keeping one small promise is part of building God’s system.
think: In Psalm 15:1-5, what marks the one who may live on God’s holy hill?
Have I recently changed plans too easily because a “better opportunity” came along?
What promise have I made but not yet kept that I need to follow through on today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, Your promises never fail. I confess that I often change my commitments for convenience or gain, and I have talked about friends behind their backs. Forgive me. Make my word carry weight, so that I do what I say, keeping my oath even when it hurts. And help me keep confidences, so that my friends can rest easy with me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, check your calendar and messages for a promise you made but haven’t kept yet. Contact the person, set a time to follow through, and do it.
lessons.quick: Faithfulness isn’t keeping your word when it’s convenient; it’s keeping it when it costs you.
text: LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?
He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart;
he who doesn’t slander with his tongue, nor does evil to his friend, nor casts slurs against his fellow man;
in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;
he who doesn’t lend out his money for usury, nor take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be shaken.

lessons.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
lessons.hear:
Naomi had lost her husband and both her sons, and she was left a destitute widow in a foreign land. She urged her two daughters-in-law to go back to their families and start over. One of them left in tears, which made perfect sense. But the other, Ruth, said, “Don’t urge me to leave you, and to return from following you, for where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

Ruth’s faithfulness wasn’t a passing emotion; it was a very costly choice: leaving her familiar homeland to walk with an elderly woman who had nothing and was full of bitterness, into an unknown future. She didn’t offer a lot of comforting explanations. She simply said: I’m not leaving. What people in trouble need most often isn’t answers; it’s someone who is there.

Today, learn from Ruth’s faithfulness. Think about who around you is living through a “Naomi season.” Maybe it’s a classmate who just lost their job, an older person who was recently widowed, a friend whom relatives and friends have drifted away from after a divorce, or a young person who fell ill while studying far from home. When trouble first hits, everyone shows concern; a month later, the messages dwindle. A faithful friend is the one who still shows up after the crowd has gone. You could send a message at the same time every week, set up a simple meal, or go with them to handle some tedious errand. Scripture says, “there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24).

At the same time, be wise. Walking alongside someone doesn’t mean taking over, and faithfulness doesn’t mean shouldering responsibilities you can’t carry. If the person is caught in long-term depression or a crisis, helping them seek counseling or medical care is the most faithful love you can show. And you need brothers and sisters to help carry the load too—don’t try to hold it all up alone.
lessons.light: Ruth’s “I’m not leaving” is selfless faithfulness: setting aside her own future to walk with someone through the valley. This is the likeness of Christ, who promised, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). Life first, then relationships: only those who have been accompanied by the Lord know how to accompany others, and how to do it for the long haul.
think: In Ruth 1:15-18, what are the “I will” statements Ruth makes?
Am I the friend who still shows up after the crowd has gone, or do I only care when trouble first hits?
This month, whom will I regularly accompany through a low season? How?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You for never leaving me in my most painful days. Give me Ruth’s heart, to stay by my friend’s side after the crowd has gone. Give me wisdom to know how to walk alongside them, and give me companions to share the load, so that the one who is in the valley experiences Your presence through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone who is going through a low season and set a weekly reminder on your phone to check in with them for a whole month. Send the first message or make the first call today.
lessons.quick: What people in trouble need most often isn’t answers; it’s someone who is there.
text: She said, “Behold, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her god. Follow your sister-in-law.”
Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you, and to return from following you, for where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD do so to me, and more also, if anything but death parts you and me.”
When Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.

lessons.title: When Demas Left
lessons.hear:
Near the end of his life, Paul wrote to Timothy from a prison in Rome. Running through his words is a deep loneliness: “for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica” (2 Timothy 4:10). Demas had once been Paul’s co-worker, named alongside Luke in the greetings of other letters. But when following Paul became dangerous and had no future, he left. Paul also says, “At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me” (2 Timothy 4:16).

Today, honestly let this passage hold up a mirror. Have I ever been someone’s Demas? When a friend got into trouble and people started talking, did I quietly leave their group chat? When a co-worker lost standing, did I stop answering their messages? When a brother fell, was I the first to pass the news along? Proverbs says, “One who brings gossip betrays a confidence, but one who is of a trustworthy spirit is one who keeps a secret” (Proverbs 11:13). Unfaithfulness sometimes isn’t about what we did, but about disappearing when we should have shown up.

Yet this passage also holds the hope of restoration. Of those who abandoned him, Paul says, “May it not be held against them” (2 Timothy 4:16). He also asks Timothy to bring Mark, who had once quit halfway. The abandoned one chooses to forgive, and the one who once failed can be trusted again. Most important of all is this line: “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:17). When everyone else had gone, the Lord had not.

The path of adjustment starts here: first admit your unfaithfulness and confess it to God. If needed, apologize to that friend and show up in their life again. And remember that we can start over because “if we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13). Our faithfulness isn’t something we hold up by our own strength; it is held up by His.
lessons.light: When Demas “loved this present world,” he stepped back from an eternal point of view to an earthly one. Self-centered friendship retreats when the cost appears; selfless faithfulness stands firm because its focus is on Jesus. Even if I have been unfaithful, the Lord still stands by me and gives me the chance to become trustworthy again. That is grace.
think: In 2 Timothy 4:9-18, who abandoned Paul? Who was still by his side?
When has someone needed me and I “disappeared,” or when have I spread what they told me?
How will I make amends with that friend and show up in their life again?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I, too, have been like Demas, leaving when a friend needed me and even spreading what they told me. Forgive me. Thank You for standing by me when everyone else left. Give me courage to make amends, and let me be held up by Your faithfulness so that I become someone people can trust. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you weren’t there for when they needed you, or whose confidence you betrayed. After confessing it to God, apologize to them by message or in person, and let them know you want to be there for them again.
lessons.quick: When everyone else has gone, the Lord still stands by me.
text: Be diligent to come to me soon,
for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; and Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.
But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come—and the books, especially the parchments.
Alexander the coppersmith did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds.
Beware of him, for he greatly opposed our words.
At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them.
But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear. So I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Wherever the King Is, I Will Be
lessons.hear:
It was the most humiliating day of David’s life. His son Absalom had rebelled, and David fled Jerusalem barefoot and weeping. Just then, David noticed a foreigner: Ittai the Gittite. Ittai had only recently come over to David’s side, and David couldn’t bear to drag him down too: “Whereas you came but yesterday, should I today make you go up and down with us, since I go where I may?” (2 Samuel 15:20). This was Ittai’s perfect chance to walk away unscathed.

But Ittai said, “As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, surely in what place my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, your servant will be there also” (2 Samuel 15:21). Faithfulness isn’t measured by how long you’ve known someone, but by where you stand when things are at their worst. Proverbs laments, “Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?” (Proverbs 20:6). On the day David lost everything, God let him find one.

This week we have seen in Jonathan a friendship that loves at all times; learned from the psalm to keep an oath even when it hurts; heard Ruth say “I’m not leaving”; seen our own unfaithfulness in Demas; and found restoration in “the Lord stood by me.” Ittai sums it all up in one sentence: wherever the king is, there I will be. This is also Jesus’ call to us: “Where I am, there my servant will also be” (John 12:26). Faithfulness to our friends is rooted in faithfulness to our King.

Notice the last verse: “Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones who were with him” (2 Samuel 15:22). One man’s faithfulness carried a whole household across the river. That is multiplication: faithfulness is seen, and it is imitated. Your children and the young people you mentor are watching how you treat a friend who has fallen on hard times.

To repeat is to remind yourself every morning: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). To multiply is to bring someone with you to “cross the river” this week: visit a friend who is in a low season together, or tell them one story of faithfulness you learned this week.
lessons.light: Ittai’s faithfulness wasn’t built on David’s success but on who the king was. Those who let Jesus reign don’t scatter when a friend loses standing. The spiritual parents-and-children relationships of 235 let the next generation see how we keep our commitments. When faithfulness is seen, it is reproduced, and it carries a whole household across the river.
think: In 2 Samuel 15:19-22, what way out did David offer Ittai, and how did Ittai answer?
When a friend loses standing, where do I stand?
Whom will I bring with me to “cross the river” this week and practice faithfulness together?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You that Your faithfulness is new every morning and that You never abandon me. Make me like Ittai, still standing by my friends at their lowest. Above all, make me a follower of Jesus: wherever He is, there I will be. And let the people around me see Your faithfulness in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a younger brother or sister, or a family member, to visit or call a friend who is going through a low season with you. On the way back, share Ittai’s story and pray for each other.
lessons.quick: Wherever the King is, I will be; faithfulness carries a whole household across the river.
text: Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why do you also go with us? Return, and stay with the king; for you are a foreigner and also an exile. Return to your own place.
Whereas you came but yesterday, should I today make you go up and down with us, since I go where I may? Return, and take back your brothers. Mercy and truth be with you.”
Ittai answered the king and said, “As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, surely in what place my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, your servant will be there also.”
David said to Ittai, “Go and pass over.” Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones who were with him.

weeks.keyText: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.

weeks.title: Gentleness: Restoring Others Gently
weeks.theme: Gentleness is not weakness but strength tamed by the Holy Spirit; a gentle answer turns away wrath.
group: Read Galatians 6:1-2. How does Paul tell “you who are spiritual” to treat someone caught in a fault?
In what situations are you most likely to speak harshly? What are you protecting in your heart at those moments?
Whom are you willing to restore or comfort with gentleness this week, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, set aside some quiet time to be with a friend who has recently stumbled, grown discouraged, or clashed with someone: invite them for a walk, a cup of tea, or a simple meal at your home. Before you go, pray that the Lord would make your heart gentle and humble. When you meet, listen more, comment less, and don’t rush to correct. Afterward, thank the Lord for the grace with which He has gently restored you.

lessons.title: Restore in a Spirit of Gentleness
lessons.hear:
Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). Notice Paul’s measure of whether someone is “spiritual.” It isn’t how good they are at pointing out other people’s mistakes, but whether they can gently bring back someone who has fallen.

The word translated “restore” could be used in Paul’s day for mending fishing nets, or for a doctor setting a dislocated bone back in place. Picture it: when setting a bone, a doctor doesn’t grab a hammer, and he doesn’t scold, “Who told you to be so careless?” while he works. His hands must be steady, precise, and light. Restoring someone who has fallen is the same; roughness only causes a second fracture.

Many people think gentleness means being weak, having no backbone, letting others push you around. But the gentleness the Bible speaks of is more like a well-trained stallion: it hasn’t lost an ounce of strength; it simply no longer charges and kicks wildly, but responds to its master’s reins. Jesus said, “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). Gentle people are not powerless; their power is in the Holy Spirit’s hands.

Paul adds two more reminders. First, “looking to yourself”: when restoring others, don’t forget that you are just as weak—today they fall, tomorrow it could be me. Second, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Gentleness isn’t just speaking softly; it means crouching down and carrying the load together with the other person. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you who around you has been caught in a fault and is waiting for a pair of gentle hands.
lessons.light: When proud people correct others, they stand up high and point down. When humble people restore others, they crouch down and help carry the load. Gentleness is returning to our proper place: I am not the judge; I, too, am a sinner who has received grace. To let Jesus reign is to let His reins govern my strength and my tongue, so that my strength becomes a strength that restores people.
think: In Galatians 6:1-2, what three things does Paul tell those who are spiritual to do?
When I face someone who has done wrong, am I more like a person with a hammer or a doctor setting a bone?
Who around me has been caught in a fault? How can I approach them gently?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You didn’t treat me roughly when I fell; You gently brought me back. Tame my strength and my tongue, so that when I face someone who has done wrong, I don’t stand above them accusing, but crouch down and help carry the load. And remind me always to look to myself, because I need You just as much as they do. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a friend who has recently made a mistake or stumbled. Without bringing up what they did wrong, send them a caring message first: “How have you been? I’d love to grab a cup of tea with you.”
lessons.quick: Restoring someone is like setting a bone: hands steady, touch light.
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.

lessons.title: A Gentle Answer Turns Away Wrath
lessons.hear:
A brother served on his apartment building’s management committee. One evening, someone in the residents’ group chat blew up over parking spaces, firing off several messages in a row and accusing the committee by name of making “backroom deals.” The brother was furious the moment he saw it. His fingers flew across the screen as he typed a long rebuttal, ending with: “If you can’t read the notice, don’t talk nonsense.” As soon as he hit send, the group chat erupted. Some people piled on, some left the group, and even residents who never posted anything started taking sides.

We often carry an old mindset: being gentle means getting walked all over; if you don’t raise your voice, people will trample you; to win an argument, you can’t back down. But Proverbs gives us God’s point of view: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Anger is like a fire. Harsh words are gasoline; gentle words are water. You get to choose which one to pour.

Proverbs also says, “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit” (Proverbs 15:4). Gentle words aren’t words without a position; they are the ability to say true things in a way the other person can actually hear. The wise man even says, “A soft tongue breaks the bone” (Proverbs 25:15). That doesn’t mean gentleness is soft; it means gentleness is more powerful than meeting force with force. It can break the hardest bone in a person’s heart.

Once the brother calmed down, he posted a new message in the group: “My tone just now was out of line, and I apologize to everyone. The parking arrangements really could be explained more clearly. Tomorrow evening we’ll go over them in person in the lobby, and everyone is welcome to share their input.” The next day, the resident who had blown up came too. The two of them talked for half an hour, and finally he said, “Honestly, I was so upset because the elderly relative living with us has trouble getting around.” The gentle answer turned away the anger and let the real need come to the surface.
lessons.light: Harsh words are pride provoking pride; a gentle answer is humility drawing out humility. People matter more than things: a parking space is a thing; a neighbor is a person. Don’t hurt people over things. Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, not the head and our own strength—the head is thinking about how to win; the Holy Spirit in our hearts is thinking about how to win the person.
think: In Proverbs 15:1-4, what results come from gentle words and from harsh words?
When was the last time I spoke harshly? What was I protecting at the time?
What potentially harsh sentence will I replace with a gentler way of saying it today?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I often try to beat others by sheer force, saying harsh things that stir up anger and wound hearts. Make my tongue a tree of life, able to speak the truth gently so that people can hear it. And help me see, beneath the anger, what the other person really needs. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, before replying to any message that upsets you, pause for one minute. Delete the sharpest sentence and replace it with a gentler way of saying it before you hit send.
lessons.quick: Harsh words are gasoline; gentle words are water. Which will you pour?
text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

lessons.title: Gentle Toward All
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote young Timothy a word that fits the internet age remarkably well: “But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife” (2 Timothy 2:23). He continues: “The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him” (2 Timothy 2:24-25).

Every day, we can get pulled into “foolish and ignorant questionings”: flame wars on social media, political topics in the family group chat, friends’ sarcastic jabs at our faith. Many Christians think that standing for the truth means never giving an inch and making every word cut. But Paul says that even “those who oppose” are to be corrected “in gentleness.” Why? Because our goal isn’t to win the argument but that “perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:25). To win the argument but lose the person is the greatest failure of all.

Today, practice using three “gentleness filters.” First, ask about purpose: am I responding to win this person, or to prove I’m right? If it’s only to win, stop. Second, ask about setting: is this something to say in a public comment thread, or in a private message—or even over coffee in person? Many conversations change temperature completely when you change the setting. Third, ask about tone: read your drafted reply once more and imagine the other person is the family member you love most. Could you still say it in that tone?

Gentleness doesn’t mean not speaking the truth. Sometimes we still need to state our position clearly, and when facing harassment or malicious attacks, we can block, leave, or get help. But even when we say “no,” we can say it with dignity and warmth. The Lord’s servant is gentle, because his Lord is too.
lessons.light: Quarreling is the self-centered life: I have to win. Gentleness is the selfless life: I would rather people see Christ than see how clever I am. The focus is on Jesus, not on who wins the argument. This week, use the app’s Word Watch to examine yourself each night: Were my words gentle today? Did I hurt anyone in order to win?
think: In 2 Timothy 2:22-26, how is the Lord’s servant to act toward those who oppose him?
Have I recently said something harsh online or in a group chat just to win?
Which “gentleness filter” will I use today on a message I feel like rebutting?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, even toward those who opposed You, You were gentle and full of truth. I confess that I often want to win the argument and forget to win the person. Help me refuse pointless quarrels and be gentle toward all; and when I need to speak the truth, help me speak it with dignity and warmth. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you come across a post or message you want to rebut, run it through the three filters first (purpose, setting, tone). If you really do need to respond, do it by private message or in person, and say it gently.
lessons.quick: To win the argument but lose the person is the greatest failure of all.
text: Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,
and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to do his will.

lessons.title: Put the Sword into Its Sheath
lessons.hear:
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter did something he thought was very brave: “Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear” (John 18:10). He thought this was loyalty—standing up for his Lord. But Jesus said to him, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?” (John 18:11).

Peter’s sword is a lot like our tongues and keyboards. We think we are defending the truth or protecting the people we love, but often we are lashing out in the flesh. When offended, we want to hit back; when misunderstood, we want to bite back; when we see injustice, we want to make the other side bleed a little first. Peter’s failure reminds us that zeal is not the same as spirituality, and impulsiveness is not the same as courage.

Yet that sword was not the end of Peter’s story. Years later, the same Peter wrote to believers under persecution: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15). The man who drew his sword learned to sheathe it; the impulsive fisherman became an apostle who taught others to answer with humility. Who changed him? The Lord who healed the servant’s ear right in front of him, and who gently restored him after he had denied Him three times.

Today, review: when does my “sword” usually come out? When I’m criticized, when I’m misunderstood, or when I see my family treated unfairly? The way to adjust is first to “sanctify the Lord God in your hearts”: before you open your mouth, let Christ reign in your heart. When Christ sits on the throne of the heart, it becomes much easier for our hands to put the sword back in its sheath.
lessons.light: Peter’s sword is self-centered zeal: standing up for the Lord in the flesh. Selfless gentleness first lets Christ reign in the heart, and only then speaks. Review, adjust, repeat—between Peter drawing his sword and Peter writing letters that teach humility lies the Lord’s gentle restoration, again and again. As He treats me, so I treat others.
think: Comparing John 18:10-11 with 1 Peter 3:15, how did Peter change?
In what situations does my “sword” usually come out?
The next time I want to hit back, how will I first “sanctify the Lord God” in my heart?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I am often like Peter, drawing my sword in the flesh and thinking I’m standing up for You. Thank You for not giving up on him, and for not giving up on me. Sit on the throne of my heart, so that before I speak I set You apart as holy, learn to put my sword back in its sheath, and answer people with humility and reverence. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, recall the last time your words “cut” someone. If they were hurt, apologize to them in a sentence. Then write out 1 Peter 3:15 and put it on your phone as a reminder.
lessons.quick: Let Christ reign in your heart first, and your hand will find it easier to sheathe the sword.
text: Now who will harm you if you become imitators of that which is good?
But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.
For it is better, if it is God’s will, that you suffer for doing what is right than for doing evil.

lessons.title: Learn from Me
lessons.hear:
In all the Gospels, there is only one place where Jesus describes His own heart in His own words, and this is what He says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). He didn’t say, “I am mighty in heart” or “I am full of wisdom in heart,” but “gentle and humble.” This is what He most wants us to know about Him.

Notice the order. Jesus first invites “all you who labor and are heavily burdened” to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28), and only then says, “learn from me.” Gentleness isn’t something we learn first by gritting our teeth; it grows after we have found rest in Him. Someone who is anxious, exhausted, and full of insecurity finds it very hard to be gentle—like a string strung too tight that snaps at a touch. Lay your burdens down with the Lord first; when your heart loosens, you can be gentle with people.

The Old Testament also records, “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). This leader who brought millions out of Egypt is remembered not only for miracles but for the meekness that kept him from defending himself when he was slandered.

This week we have seen that gentleness is tamed strength; learned that a gentle answer turns away wrath; practiced being gentle toward all; and seen ourselves in Peter’s sword. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat is to go to the Lord each morning and lay down your burdens before going out to face people. To multiply is to model gentleness for the people around you: replace yelling with gentleness at home and correction with gentleness in your small group, so that your children, coworkers, and group members see the Lord’s likeness in you. Paul says, “Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand” (Philippians 4:5).
lessons.light: The source of gentleness is rest: those who have been caught by the Lord’s love no longer need sharp edges to protect themselves. This is change from the inside out—first lay down the burden in your heart; when your life softens, your relationships soften. Jesus is my example. His yoke is easy, and His way is worth a lifetime of learning.
think: In Matthew 11:28-30, how does Jesus describe His heart? What does He invite us to do?
Is my sharpness a sign that my heart is too tired and too tense?
In front of whom will I model the Lord’s gentle and humble way this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are gentle and humble in heart. I lay my labor and my burdens on You; let my soul find rest in You. And as my heart softens, help me treat my family, coworkers, and small group with gentleness, so that they see Your likeness in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tomorrow morning before you head out, take five minutes to hand the day’s burdens to the Lord. This week, choose a family member or group member, replace your usual impatient response with one gentle action, and share this insight with them.
lessons.quick: Find rest in the Lord first; then you can be gentle with people.
text: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

weeks.keyText: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.

weeks.title: Self-Control: Ruling Your Spirit
weeks.theme: Self-control means letting the Holy Spirit govern my emotions, words, and desires, so that a moment’s impulse doesn’t tear down a relationship.
group: Read Proverbs 16:32. Why is ruling your spirit harder—and worth more—than taking a city?
What is hardest for you to control: your emotions, your words, or a particular desire? How does it affect your relationships?
In which relationship will you practice self-control this week for the other person’s good, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, try a digital Sabbath: choose half a day to put your phone away and give your full attention to your family or a friend—take a walk, cook, or simply talk together. Before you start, pray and offer your time and attention to the Lord. Afterward, reflect: with less time spent scrolling, whom did you see more clearly? Thank God for it.

lessons.title: Grace Teaches Us to Live Soberly
lessons.hear:
Solomon says, “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). In the ancient world, capturing a city was the greatest of achievements; it took troops, strategy, and courage. But Solomon says there is one battle harder than taking a city: ruling your own spirit. Many people can manage a department, a family, or a business, yet can’t manage one remark that flies out of their mouth, one late-night urge to hit “buy,” or one surge of anger that wants to talk back in the group chat.

Where does self-control come from? Many people think it means gritting your teeth and holding on by willpower. But Paul tells Titus, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age” (Titus 2:11-12). Notice that the teacher who instructs us to live soberly isn’t the whip of the law but grace.

That is wonderful news. Self-control powered by willpower is like holding down a spring with your hand: the moment you let go, it shoots up even higher. Self-control powered by grace is like a person so filled with love that they no longer need to find security in food, shopping, other people’s praise, or winning arguments. When your heart is satisfied, you don’t have to grab at everything. Paul goes on to say that Christ “gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). We have been redeemed not only out of sin, but so that we can freely love others.

In our relationships, self-control has three battlefields: emotions, words, and desires. Emotions out of control wound people; words out of control drive people apart; desires out of control use people. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to be the watchman on the walls of your heart and to show you which impulse needs to be handed over to the Lord.
lessons.light: The self-centered person is dragged around by emotions and desires, because whatever “I” want, I want right now. The selfless person lets the Holy Spirit govern, because the heart already has the Lord as King. Self-control isn’t suppression but surrender; it isn’t holding on with the head but using the heart and relying on the Holy Spirit—being instructed by grace and letting Jesus reign in the heart.
think: In Titus 2:11-14, who instructs us to live soberly, and for what purpose?
On which battlefield—emotions, words, or desires—do I most often lose ground?
