Which impulse will I hand over to the Lord first today?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You that Your grace has appeared, not only forgiving me but also instructing me to live soberly. I confess that I am often dragged around by my emotions, my words, and my desires, and I have hurt the people around me. Be Lord of my heart, so that instead of white-knuckling it by willpower, I am filled with Your love and free to rule my spirit. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pick the impulse you give in to most often (talking back, late-night scrolling, impulse buying). When it shows up, pause for ten seconds and silently pray, “Lord, You are in charge,” before deciding whether to act.
lessons.quick: Ruling your spirit beats taking a city; what teaches us self-control is grace, not the whip.
text: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;
looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ,
who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.

lessons.title: “That’s Just How I Am”?
lessons.hear:
A mom who was very active in her child’s class parents’ group chat was proud of being “a straight shooter.” If the teacher dropped the ball on something, she was the first to blast them in the group. If other parents disagreed with her, she would screenshot their messages and forward them to others to “let them be the judge.” She often said, “That’s just how I am. I say what I think—better than stabbing people in the back.” Until one day she discovered that her child was being shunned by classmates, because other parents had been saying privately, “Keep your distance from that mom.”

We often carry an old mindset: it’s healthy to vent your emotions; this is my personality, and people need to accept it; being authentic is better than being fake-polite. But Proverbs gives us God’s point of view: “A perverse man stirs up strife. A whisperer separates close friends” (Proverbs 16:28). Dumping your emotions on others and forwarding your complaints around isn’t called “being authentic”; it’s called stirring up strife. Solomon goes on: “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty” (Proverbs 16:32). The truly strong person is the one who can govern themselves.

This doesn’t mean we should bottle up our emotions and pretend everything is fine. The Psalms are full of David’s anger, grief, and complaints—but he poured them out before God, not in the group chat. Emotions themselves are not sin; what matters is where we pour them. Speak to God first, then decide what to say to people, how to say it, and where.

Later, that mom tearfully shared the whole story in her small group. She began practicing a small habit: whenever she wanted to blow up in the group chat, she first typed her words into a notes app, “said” them to God, and looked at them again the next day. Eight times out of ten, she ended up deleting them. The other two times, she turned them into a private message to the teacher, in a much gentler tone. A few months later, she had become one of the most trusted parents in the group. Personality is no excuse, because the Holy Spirit can change our personality.
lessons.light: “That’s just how I am” is the self-centered life’s excuse: it expects others to accommodate me instead of letting God change me. The selfless person admits they need to be changed. Change the mindset and the life changes: once I believe the Holy Spirit can change my personality, I stop making excuses for my impulses and hand them over to Him.
think: In Proverbs 16:27-32, who damages relationships, and who is praised?
Have I ever used “that’s just how I am” to defend my impulses?
The next time my emotions rise, where will I “pour” my words first?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often use “my personality” as an excuse to dump my emotions on others, stirring up strife. Forgive me. Teach me to pour out my anger and hurt before You first, and then to decide wisely what to say to people. And help me believe that Your Holy Spirit can change my personality. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, whenever you feel like blowing up in a group chat or conversation, type your words into a notes app first, say them to God, and decide the next day whether to delete them, turn them into a private message, or say them gently.
lessons.quick: Emotions aren’t sin; what matters is where you pour them.
text: A worthless man devises mischief. His speech is like a scorching fire.
A perverse man stirs up strife. A whisperer separates close friends.
A man of violence entices his neighbor, and leads him in a way that is not good.
One who winks his eyes to plot perversities, one who compresses his lips, is bent on evil.
Gray hair is a crown of glory. It is attained by a life of righteousness.
One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

lessons.title: A City Without Walls
lessons.hear:
Proverbs 25 has a vivid line: “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint” (Proverbs 25:28). In the ancient world, a city’s walls protected the people inside and determined what could come in and what had to be kept out. A person without self-control is like a city without walls: any emotion, temptation, or pressure can march straight in, and the people inside may rush out at any moment and hurt someone.

Interestingly, this chapter of Proverbs talks about self-control in very everyday terms. “Have you found honey? Eat as much as is sufficient for you” (Proverbs 25:16)—at meals and social events, eat and drink in moderation, and when someone keeps pushing drinks on you, you can gently say no. “Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor’s house, lest he be weary of you, and hate you” (Proverbs 25:17)—even the best relationships need a sense of proportion: don’t bombard people with messages, don’t show up uninvited, don’t treat your friends as an emotional dumping ground. “It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it honorable to seek one’s own honor” (Proverbs 25:27)—don’t spend every gathering talking about your achievements, and don’t post just to fish for likes.

Today, choose one specific stretch of “wall” to repair. First, your mouth: at this gathering, ask more about how others are doing and say less about yourself. Second, your hands: before sending a message today, think—is this a good time for them? Have I already sent too many? Third, your eyes: set aside a digital Sabbath time slot for yourself, and trade your scrolling time for being present with the people in front of you.

In relationships, self-control is really a form of respect: respect for other people’s time, space, and feelings. A person with walls actually makes others feel safer coming close, because they know you won’t lose control or overstep.
lessons.light: Self-control is the shape of love: it doesn’t just restrain me; it respects others. The proud “seek their own honor” and need to be seen everywhere; the humble know their proper measure and make room for others. When the walls of the heart are rebuilt, the people in our relationships can dwell securely, and love can go the distance.
think: What kinds of things needing self-control does Proverbs 25:16-17, 27-28 mention?
In eating and drinking, visiting, messaging, or talking about myself—where have I overstepped?
Which stretch of “wall” will I repair today? How, specifically?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that my heart is often like a city without walls: emotions and desires march straight in, and I often overstep and intrude on others. Help me rebuild my walls: govern my mouth, my hands, and my eyes; help me respect other people’s time and space, so that people feel safe around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, at a gathering or in a group chat, practice “one more question about others, one less sentence about myself.” And set an hour tonight as a digital Sabbath, giving that time to your family or roommates.
lessons.quick: A person with walls actually makes others feel safer coming close.
text: Have you found honey? Eat as much as is sufficient for you, lest you eat too much, and vomit it.
Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor’s house, lest he be weary of you, and hate you.
It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it honorable to seek one’s own honor.
Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.

lessons.title: Abigail Stopped Me
lessons.hear:
David lost control too. He and his men had protected Nabal’s shepherds and flocks in the wilderness, yet at sheep-shearing time Nabal insulted him and refused to give him any food. David’s anger flared instantly: “He has returned me evil for good” (1 Samuel 25:21). He swore before God that by morning not one male belonging to Nabal would be left alive (see 1 Samuel 25:22). A man anointed by God, the author of many psalms, came within a hair of slaughtering an entire household because he had been insulted once.

This passage helps us see honestly that our self-control usually gives way not over big things but in the moment we are humiliated, looked down on, or repaid evil for our kindness. In that moment, our anger feels entirely justified—we can even put it into words like “He has returned me evil for good.” It is just as Cain was warned: “sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it” (Genesis 4:7).

God used Abigail to stop David. She came out to meet him humbly, bringing gifts, and reminded him not to let taking revenge with his own hand become a lifelong stain. And David did something remarkable: he listened. “Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand” (1 Samuel 25:33). Someone who can stop in the middle of a rage, listen to counsel, and change direction—that is a true mighty man.

Today, review this way: who is the “Abigail” God has placed in my life? Perhaps a spouse, a close friend, a small group leader, or the still, small voice of the Holy Spirit in your heart. When they say, “Hold on, don’t do anything rash,” do I listen, or do I get even angrier? The way to adjust is to have an Abigail ready for yourself—ask someone to remind you when you’re worked up—and to be willing to gently be an Abigail for others when they are losing control.
lessons.light: David’s anger was a self-centered reaction: “He has returned me evil for good,” with all the focus on the wrong done to me. The selfless person can still listen and stop, even in anger. The spiritual companions of 235 are Abigails for one another: when the other is about to lose control, they step in, courageously and gently, so that neither leaves behind a lifelong regret.
think: In 1 Samuel 25, what did David say before and after his rage? What made him stop?
In what situations am I most likely to lose control? When someone has tried to counsel me then, how did I react?
Who can be my “Abigail”? And whose Abigail can I be?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I, too, have wanted to settle the score with my own hand when I was insulted or looked down on. Thank You for the Abigails You have placed in my life, and for the still, small voice of the Holy Spirit. Give me a heart that is willing to listen, so that I can stop in the middle of my anger; and make me able to gently be someone else’s Abigail. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a spiritual companion you trust. Ask them to remind you to “pause for a moment” when your emotions are running high, and agree that you will do the same for them. Pray for each other.
lessons.quick: Someone who can stop mid-rage and listen to counsel is a true mighty man.
text: Now David had said, “Surely in vain I have kept all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained to him. He has returned me evil for good.
God do so to the enemies of David, and more also, if I leave of all that belongs to him by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

For indeed, as the LORD the God of Israel lives, who has withheld me from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there wouldn’t have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
So David received from her hand that which she had brought him. Then he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. Behold, I have listened to your voice and have granted your request.”

lessons.title: In Knowledge, Self-Control
lessons.hear:
Peter lays out a ladder of spiritual growth: “in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge; and in knowledge, self-control; and in self-control, perseverance” (2 Peter 1:5-6), climbing all the way up to “in godliness, brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love” (2 Peter 1:7). Notice that self-control sits in the middle of the ladder. It comes after knowledge, because knowing the right thing isn’t enough; you also need the strength to do it. And it comes before perseverance, because someone who can’t govern themselves will struggle to bear with others for the long haul.

The top of the ladder is love. Self-control isn’t about making ourselves look disciplined; it’s about being able to love people well. A father who can’t control his temper will hurt his children no matter how much he loves them; a friend who can’t control their tongue will hurt their friends no matter how much they mean well. Self-control is the guardrail that keeps love from going off course.

With this, our journey through the fruit of the Spirit in our relationships comes to a close. We have learned about love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and today, self-control. Paul says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23)—where “faith” here means faithfulness. Notice that it is “fruit,” not nine techniques: nine expressions of one life, which is Christ Himself in us.

Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat is to ask yourself each night before bed, “Today, which fruit grew toward whom? Which one is still green and unripe?” To multiply is to share this journey through the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit with a spiritual companion and invite them to practice it with you. Because “God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7), we can keep climbing, step by step, with hope.
lessons.light: The “9” of 920 isn’t nine words to memorize but the fruit Christ’s life bears through each “2”; the “0” is getting myself out of the way so the Holy Spirit can work. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: once the nine-fold fruit has grown, everything that follows—our words, boundaries, friendships, and hospitality—has a source of living water.
think: In 2 Peter 1:5-8, where does self-control sit on the ladder of growth, and what is at the top?
Looking back over the nine-fold fruit, which one is the least ripe in me?
With which companion will I share this journey through the nine-fold fruit, inviting them to practice with me?
lessons.speak: Father, thank You for leading me, one by one, to know the fruit of the Spirit these past weeks. I confess that some of this fruit is still green in me, but I trust that Your life is in me. Help me rule my spirit so that love doesn’t go off course; and give me companions to bear the fruit of Christ together in every relationship. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, meet with a spiritual companion. Each of you share which fruit has grown the most and which most needs prayer, and pray for each other. You might also add a card for them in the app’s 920 Relationship Map and write down your prayer requests.
lessons.quick: Nine expressions, one life: Christ in me.
text: Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge;
and in knowledge, self-control; and in self-control, perseverance; and in perseverance, godliness;
and in godliness, brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love.
For if these things are yours and abound, they make you to not be idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
